How to Use This Guide

This is a repository, not a manual. Most subjects are a ranked shelf: find the subject, pick a resource at the tier and in the dimension that fits what you need, and tick the box once you've worked through it. Everything is sorted best-first within tier.

Use the category chips (Computing, Math & Sciences…) to show only the areas you care about; your choice is remembered. Every subject opens with its Optimal path: the stages to work through in order, each with one Main resource (whichever course or book teaches that stage best), plus a short First intuition-builder and a place to Practise where they help. Below it sit two collapsed alternatives: the Course path (course-led, with companion reads; switch it to Courses or Books) and the Textbook path (books only). Within every topic, the first row is the Start here pick — badged Main — the single best place to begin. Then come three lanes: Courses, Books & readings ranked best-first, and Extras (narratives, podcasts and fiction) to enjoy on the side. Use the Hide textbooks and Hide extras filters to strip a lane out.

One rule everywhere: within each lane, rows are ranked best-first — start at the top and stop when you have what you need. Where subject-matter order matters (pre-calculus before calculus, fundamentals before theory), the topic groups themselves are arranged in learning order — work the groups top to bottom.

Tiers

■ Essential — read this to own the subject. The 202 Essentials are the curriculum; everything else is elaboration.

■ Recommended — deepen or complement.

■ Optional — reference or elite-tier.

Dimensions

Textbook · Narrative · Fiction · Course · Video · Interactive · Website · Article · Podcast · Problems/Drill · Reference · Primary · Survey · Code — the kind of resource, so you can pick the mode that fits how you want to learn a topic (e.g. a narrative to fall in love with a field, a textbook to master it, problems to prove it).

Editorial Charter — what this guide is & how it decides

This charter records what the guide is for and how it makes decisions, so its standards stay consistent as it grows. Read it before adding, cutting, or re-ranking anything.

Purpose

A curated best-of, not an index. The guide answers “what is the most effective way to learn X?” It is a ranked repository of the finest resources per subject — deliberately selective. Completeness is never the goal; quality and pedagogy are. If a resource isn’t among the best-taught or most illuminating for its topic, it doesn’t belong, however famous or free it is.

Learn smarter, not harder. Favor resources that build intuition, teach by doing, and are genuinely beloved for how well they teach — over exhaustive, rigor-for-its-own-sake, or merely canonical texts. All formats are welcome and equal in principle: books, courses, video, interactive sites, blogs, podcasts. Pick the format that teaches a given topic best.

Breadth of a whole education. The scope is the sciences, mathematics, and computing; the humanities — philosophy, history, literature; the practical crafts of building; and the transferable arts of learning, clear thinking, and judgment. The unifying test isn’t the subject but the aim: does this help someone understand the world more deeply or think more clearly? Wisdom and competence count alongside raw knowledge — which is why great lives, decision science, and a curiosity layer earn their place.

What it values

Pedagogy above prestige. The best teacher of a topic beats the most authoritative reference. A gentle, vivid, intuition-first resource outranks a comprehensive but forbidding one.

Quality is the only ranking axis — cost is not. Resources are judged purely on how well they teach. Whether a resource is free or paid is deliberately not tracked anywhere in this guide: cost never affects inclusion, ranking, or a resource's rationale.

Every format, deployed where it teaches best. A narrative to fall in love with a field; a textbook to master it; problems to prove it; a course or video for a guided path; an interactive site to explore. The dimension tag exists so a learner can pick the mode that fits their need.

A curiosity layer, on purpose. Beloved popular-science and “fall in love with the subject” books earn a place (the Curiosity Shelf and narrative picks) — momentum and wonder are part of learning, not a distraction from it.

What it avoids

No fluff. Exclude self-help, productivity-hacking, habits/lifestyle, business, leadership, and career books — even when a source everyone respects recommends them — unless a work is genuinely gold-standard: evidence-based, substantive, and true. This is a guide to learning subjects, not to life optimization.

No rigor-for-its-own-sake. Graduate reference texts prized mainly for exhaustiveness or austerity (the classic “impressive but forbidding” canon) are deliberately left out unless they are also genuinely well-taught. Depth is welcome; hazing is not.

Wonder and intellectual fiction are welcome. Amazement is fuel: a book or channel that leaves you awed by a real subject earns its place, provided it is accurate. Fiction of ideas — hard science fiction, mathematical and scientific novels, plays and stories that make you think (Chiang, Egan, Stephenson, Gibson, Stoppard) — sits on the Curiosity Shelf alongside the popular science. What stays out is disconnected trivia and bathroom-reader fact lists: the test is whether you come away seeing a subject more clearly or wanting to learn it properly.

No dated dogma; no lateral duplicates. Resources whose central claims are discredited or superseded are removed, not kept for literacy. (Primary sources in philosophy, history and literature are read as primary texts and are exempt; a live but contested scholarly thesis may stay if its why says so plainly.) Don’t add a second resource that merely duplicates one already covered — add only if it teaches meaningfully better or fills a real gap. One work, one canonical title, one tier.

How it’s ranked & structured

One start-here per topic. Every topic group has exactly one Main — the best first resource — and it always holds the group’s highest tier, so the badge and the tier never disagree.

Three tiers, best-first. Essential (own the subject), Recommended (deepen or complement), Optional (reference or elite-tier). Within every group, resources are ordered best-first by pedagogical value. Tier encodes quality — so a lower-quality-but-worthwhile resource simply sits lower, rather than being excluded.

Grouped by topic for scanning. Larger subjects are split into topic clusters (tinted sub-headers) so a learner can find the best resource for a sub-topic at a glance. Small, single-theme subjects stay flat. Each resource carries a one-line “why” that states its teaching merit.

Cross-list only when genuinely dual-purpose. A resource may appear in two sections when it truly serves both (e.g. a systems text that anchors both CS and system design). Otherwise, one home, chosen by primary discipline.

How to develop it (method)

Read the primary source, not a summary. When mining a guide, syllabus, article, or repo, work from the actual source — summaries and research digests reliably capture the technical spine but drop the accessible / popular-book / curiosity layers, and can’t catch sources that changed since. This has burned this guide repeatedly. For one navigable authoritative source, go straight to it. For topics scattered across the web, research first to discover, then verify the shortlist against the real sources before adding. If a page is blocked or won’t load, say so plainly and get the real text — never reconstruct a list from memory and present it as read.

A source recommending a book is not the bar — fit is. Distinguished sources (a famous list, a respected blog, a great mathematician) make a candidate worth checking, not worth importing wholesale. A pull-quote is not an endorsement. Judge every candidate against this guide’s own purpose, which is often a different audience than the source had in mind.

Apply the charter as a filter, not a funnel. For every candidate, ask: is this among the best-taught or most illuminating for its topic, and does it fit a lane the guide serves? Most well-known resources that clear a low bar should still be declined — curation means saying no far more than yes. Self-help, productivity, business, and pop-persuasion are declined even when a respected source recommends them.

Rank down rather than exclude; flag when a companion is needed. A solid-but-reference-grade or lower-quality resource can be documented at a lower tier rather than dropped — tier carries the honesty. For a landmark work that is important but genuinely impenetrable (e.g. Hegel), include it with a “why” that says so and points to a companion/course — the entry then doubles as a reminder to find the best explainer. Never let an entry imply a forbidding primary text is a good on-ramp.

Verify before shipping. After any change, confirm the data parses, no resource is orphaned from its group, counts are intact, and the intended entries actually render. A correct earlier decision shouldn’t be quietly reversed by a later edit.

Learning, Writing & Research

0 / 8 Essentials · 0 / 32

The meta-skills: how to learn, read, reason, research and write. Install these first; they make every other subject faster and your conclusions more trustworthy.

Optimal path 9 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. How learning worksFirstStudy Less, Study Smart — Marty LobdellMainLearning How to Learn — Barbara Oakley & Terrence SejnowskiAlsoMake It Stick — Brown, Roediger & McDanielWatch Lobdell's one-hour lecture tonight for a quick win. Then take Oakley's short course, especially the procrastination material; read Make It Stick for the evidence behind retrieval, spacing and interleaving.
  2. Spaced repetition habitMainHow to Write Good Prompts: Using Spaced Repetition to Create Understanding — Andy MatuschakAlsoImproving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques — Dunlosky et al.PracticeAnki — Damien ElmesRead Matuschak before making cards, then start Anki with a few cards a day from everything you study. Skim Dunlosky's ratings to see why practice testing and spacing win.
  3. Reading hard booksMainHow to Read a Book — Adler & Van DorenAlsoHow to Read a Paper — KeshavLearn Adler's inspectional and analytical reading, and practise them on your next nonfiction book. Use Keshav's three-pass method whenever you open a research paper.
  4. Reasoning and argumentMainThink Again: How to Reason and Argue — Walter Sinnott-Armstrong & Ram Neta (Duke)Work through the four short courses and their quizzes: reconstruct arguments, then deduction, induction and fallacies. Practise by mapping one argument from your own reading each week.
  5. Judging evidenceMainCalling Bullshit — Carl Bergstrom & Jevin West (University of Washington)AlsoStatistics Done Wrong — Alex ReinhartWatch one Calling Bullshit lecture per evening and try its case studies. Read Statistics Done Wrong alongside for the statistical errors behind misleading research claims.
  6. Asking research questionsMainThe Craft of Research — Booth, Colomb & WilliamsRead it with a real question of your own: turn a topic into a question, a question into a claim, and gather evidence. Apply each chapter to your own project as you go.
  7. Clear writingFirstThe Craft of Writing Effectively — Larry McEnerney (University of Chicago)MainOn Writing Well — ZinsserPracticeWriting in the Sciences — Kristin Sainani (Stanford)Watch McEnerney's lecture first: writing must create value for readers. Read Zinsser quickly for plain voice; then use Sainani's editing exercises to cut clutter from your own drafts.
  8. Sentence-level revisionMainStyle: Lessons in Clarity and Grace — Joseph WilliamsWork one lesson at a time and do its revision exercises, then apply the diagnostics to a document you actually wrote this week. Slow, deliberate practice here pays off most.
  9. Doing consequential workMainThe Art of Doing Science and Engineering — Richard HammingA capstone: read a chapter per session and note what it implies for your own choice of problems, learning habits and career. Revisit yearly.
Course path 10 steps
  1. CourseLearning How to Learn — Barbara Oakley & Terrence SejnowskiBookMake It Stick — Brown, Roediger & McDanielWarm up with Lobdell's one-hour Study Less, Study Smart lecture. Then take Oakley's short course; read Make It Stick for the evidence on retrieval, spacing and interleaving.
  2. CourseThe Learning Scientists — Yana Weinstein, Megan Sumeracki et al.BookImproving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques — Dunlosky et al.Read Dunlosky's ratings: practice testing and spacing win, rereading and highlighting lose. Use the Learning Scientists' guides to turn the winning strategies into weekly routines.
  3. CourseAnki — Damien ElmesBookHow to Write Good Prompts: Using Spaced Repetition to Create Understanding — Andy MatuschakRead Matuschak before making cards, then start Anki with a few cards a day from everything you study. Keep the daily review going for the whole path.
  4. BookHow to Read a Paper — KeshavLearn the three-pass method: skim for structure, read for content, then reconstruct. Practise it on every paper later in this path.
  5. CourseThink Again: How to Reason and Argue — Walter Sinnott-Armstrong & Ram Neta (Duke)Work the four short courses and quizzes: reconstructing arguments, deduction, induction, fallacies. Each week, map one argument from your own reading.
  6. CourseCalling Bullshit — Carl Bergstrom & Jevin West (University of Washington)BookWhy Most Published Research Findings Are False — John IoannidisOne lecture per evening, trying its case studies. Read Ioannidis with Keshav's three passes to see why small, flexible studies produce false positives.
  7. CourseHow to Write a Great Research Paper — Simon Peyton JonesPick a real question from your work and start writing about it now: Peyton Jones argues writing is how research gets done, not how it is reported.
  8. CourseWriting in the Sciences — Kristin Sainani (Stanford)Watch McEnerney's lecture The Craft of Writing Effectively first: writing must create value for readers. Then do Sainani's editing exercises on your own drafts.
  9. BookThe Sense of Style — Steven PinkerWhy clear sentences work, from how readers process them. After each chapter, revise a document you wrote this week using its diagnostics.
  10. BookDraft No. 4 — John McPheeMove from sentences to whole pieces: how McPhee plans structure, drafts and revises. Outline your next long document before writing it.
Textbook path 6 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. How to Read a Book — Adler & Van DorenYour reading method: inspect a book first, then read it analytically, then compare across books. Read Part Two closely and apply it to every serious text.
  2. The Craft of Research — Booth, Colomb & WilliamsTurn a topic into a question, a question into a claim, and evidence into an argument readers trust. Use its chapters as a checklist for your own write-ups.
  3. Statistics Done Wrong — Alex ReinhartA short, intuition-first tour of statistical mistakes — p-values, power, multiple comparisons — so you can judge the evidence The Craft of Research asks you to weigh.
  4. On Writing Well — ZinsserYour first writing book: cut clutter, find a plain voice and write clear nonfiction. Quick and warm — read it straight through, then reread chapters as you write.
  5. Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace — Joseph WilliamsThe deeper sentence-level step after Zinsser: diagnose and revise prose for clarity, cohesion and emphasis, one principle per lesson. Do the exercises on your own drafts.
  6. The Art of Doing Science and Engineering — Richard HammingA capstone on learning to learn and doing consequential work: style of thinking, choosing problems, building vision. Read a chapter at a time and reflect.

Where value diverges

Learning books vary widely in evidence. Retrieval practice and spacing are the best-supported techniques (see Dunlosky et al.); deliberate-practice and 'learning hack' claims are weaker, so this shelf leads with the research and leaves out the self-optimisation genre. On style, Williams and Pinker replace Strunk & White's rule list, much of which is unsupported by actual usage.

Mathematics

0 / 22 Essentials · 0 / 164

Master this stack and any technical field reads fluently; it is the prerequisite for Physics, CS, AI and Economics. Groups run in learning order: pre-calculus, proofs, calculus, linear algebra and probability first, then the pure and applied branches, each entered at its Main. Run Math Academy daily alongside and work the problems, because mathematics is learned by doing.

Optimal path 16 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Precalculus foundationsMainPrecalculus: Mathematics for Calculus — Stewart, Redlin & WatsonAlsoPrealgebra, Intermediate Algebra & Precalculus — Professor LeonardPracticeMath AcademyPlace into Math Academy and do a lesson most evenings for the whole path. Read each Stewart, Redlin & Watson section and work odd exercises; watch Leonard whenever a topic won't click.
  2. Trigonometry and geometryMainTrigonometry: A Clever Study Guide — TantonAlsoIntroduction to Geometry — Richard Rusczyk (Art of Problem Solving)PracticeKhan Academy — Arithmetic to PrecalculusRead Tanton alongside Stewart, Redlin & Watson's trigonometry chapters; drill the unit circle and identities in Khan Academy. Work Rusczyk's geometry only where triangles and circles feel shaky; otherwise skip it.
  3. Logic and proofFirstIntroduction to Mathematical Thinking — DevlinMainHow to Prove It — VellemanAlsoProofs — CummingsPracticeNatural Number Game — Kevin BuzzardTake Devlin's short course first to see how mathematicians read definitions. Then work Velleman chapter by chapter with exercises, reading Cummings alongside for induction, combinatorial proof and cardinality; play the Natural Number Game for instant-feedback proof practice.
  4. Discrete mathematicsMainDiscrete Mathematics with Applications — Susanna EppAlsoMIT 6.1200J (OCW: 6.042J) — Mathematics for Computer Science — MITPracticeProject EulerRead Epp for counting, recursion and graphs, skimming logic Velleman already covered. Watch selected 6.042J lectures for the computer-science angle; solve Project Euler problems in code to apply it.
  5. Calculus intuitionFirstEssence of Calculus — 3Blue1BrownMainCalculus Made Easy — Silvanus P. ThompsonWatch Essence of Calculus over a weekend, then read Calculus Made Easy across a few evenings. The goal is a relaxed, intuitive grip on derivatives and integrals before the full textbook.
  6. Single-variable calculusMainCalculus — StewartAlsoCalculus 1–3 — Professor LeonardPracticePaul's Online Math Notes — Paul DawkinsWork Stewart's single-variable chapters with plenty of exercises. Watch Leonard's Calculus 1 and 2 lectures when a section needs a patient walkthrough; drill extra problems from Paul's notes. Keep Math Academy running.
  7. Linear algebraFirstEssence of Linear Algebra — 3Blue1BrownMainMIT 18.06 — Linear Algebra — Gilbert Strang (MIT)AlsoIntroduction to Linear Algebra — StrangWatch Essence of Linear Algebra first. Then per topic: one 18.06 lecture, the matching section of Strang's textbook, then the problem set. Strang's live teaching is the clearest voice here.
  8. Multivariable calculusFirstCalculus BLUE / FLCT — Robert GhristMainMIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus — Denis Auroux (MIT)Watch an 18.02 lecture, then do its problem set. Use Ghrist's Calculus BLUE for the matrix picture; reread Stewart's multivariable chapters or Leonard's Calculus 3 when you need worked examples.
  9. Probability as reasoningFirstSeeing Theory — Brown UniversityMainStat 110 — Blitzstein (Harvard)AlsoIntroduction to Probability — Blitzstein & HwangPlay with Seeing Theory's distributions first. Then per topic: one Stat 110 lecture, the matching Blitzstein & Hwang chapter, and the strategic practice problems before checking solutions.
  10. Statistical inferenceFirstStatQuest — Josh StarmerMainProbability and Statistics (4th ed.) — DeGroot & SchervishWork DeGroot & Schervish's estimation, interval, testing and regression chapters with exercises. Before each new idea, watch the matching StatQuest video for a short, plain-language picture.
  11. Bayesian and causal modellingMainStatistical Rethinking — Richard McElreathWatch one McElreath lecture, read the matching book chapter, then fit the models yourself in code and do the homework problems. This is where inference becomes a hands-on modelling skill.
  12. Differential equationsFirstDifferential Equations series — 3Blue1BrownMainMIT 18.03 — Differential Equations — Arthur Mattuck (MIT)PracticeOrdinary Differential Equations — Tenenbaum & PollardWatch the 3Blue1Brown series for the picture of phase space. Then follow Mattuck's 18.03 lectures and problem sets; drill each method in Tenenbaum & Pollard's fully worked examples.
  13. Nonlinear dynamics and chaosMainNonlinear Dynamics and Chaos — StrogatzAlsoNonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (Cornell lectures) — Steven StrogatzRead Strogatz chapter by chapter, sketching phase portraits by hand and doing exercises. If you prefer hearing a topic first, watch the matching Cornell lecture; it follows the book.
  14. Linear algebra, second passMainLinear Algebra Done Right — AxlerWith proofs now comfortable, rebuild linear algebra abstractly: vector spaces, linear maps, eigenvalues, inner products. Work the exercises; this is the bridge into analysis and abstract algebra.
  15. Real analysisFirstHow to Think About Analysis — AlcockMainUnderstanding Analysis — AbbottAlsoReal Analysis (Math 131) — Francis Su, Harvey MuddRead Alcock before or during Abbott's first chapters to learn how to handle definitions. Then work Abbott's exercises; watch Su's lectures when you want proof-writing habits modelled live.
  16. Abstract algebraFirstVisual Group Theory — Nathan CarterMainA Book of Abstract Algebra — PinterAlsoAbstract Algebra (Math E-222) — Benedict Gross, HarvardRead Visual Group Theory's early chapters to see groups as pictures. Then work Pinter chapter by chapter, exercises included; watch Gross's lectures for the big picture.
Then, by interest

Course path 15 steps
  1. CourseMath AcademyYour daily practice engine: place in at your level and do a lesson most evenings for the whole path.
  2. CoursePrealgebra, Intermediate Algebra & Precalculus — Professor LeonardAlgebra, functions, exponentials, logs and trigonometry, every example worked on the board. Pause and work each one yourself.
  3. CourseKhan Academy — Arithmetic to PrecalculusDrill trigonometry (the unit circle, graphs and identities) until it is automatic.
  4. CourseIntroduction to Mathematical Thinking — DevlinHow mathematicians read definitions and write proofs. Do this before any proof-based course.
  5. CourseMIT 6.1200J (OCW: 6.042J) — Mathematics for Computer Science — MITLogic, counting, graphs and induction: the discrete maths computer science builds on.
  6. CourseCalculus 1–3 — Professor LeonardCalculus 1 and 2 now, after a weekend with 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Calculus for the intuition. Leave Calculus 3 for the multivariable step.
  7. CourseMIT 18.06 — Linear Algebra — Gilbert Strang (MIT)Watch 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra first. Then one Strang lecture at a time, followed by its problem set.
  8. CourseMIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus — Denis Auroux (MIT)Multivariable and vector calculus, now with matrices in hand. Leonard’s Calculus 3 is the gentler alternative if you prefer his pace.
  9. CourseStat 110 — Blitzstein (Harvard)Probability as reasoning: one lecture, then every strategic practice set before checking solutions.
  10. CourseMIT 18.650 — Statistics for Applications — Philippe Rigollet (MIT)From probability to inference: estimation, confidence intervals, tests and regression.
  11. CourseStatistical Rethinking — Richard McElreathBayesian modelling and causal thinking. Fit every model yourself in code.
  12. CourseMIT 18.03 — Differential Equations — Arthur Mattuck (MIT)Linear ODEs, oscillators, Laplace transforms and systems. 3Blue1Brown’s differential-equations videos give the picture first.
  13. CourseNonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (Cornell lectures) — Steven StrogatzThe geometric view of ODEs: phase portraits, bifurcations and chaos.
  14. CourseReal Analysis (Math 131) — Francis Su, Harvey MuddRigorous calculus, taught with unusual clarity and warmth: the gateway to higher mathematics.
  15. CourseAbstract Algebra (Math E-222) — Benedict Gross, HarvardGroups, rings and fields.
Textbook path 15 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Precalculus: Mathematics for Calculus — Stewart, Redlin & WatsonYour foundation: algebra, functions, exponentials, logarithms and full trigonometry, each idea shown in a worked example first. Do the odd-numbered exercises and check answers.
  2. Trigonometry: A Clever Study Guide — TantonRead alongside Stewart, Redlin & Watson's trigonometry chapters: a short, visual book that builds the identities from a few unit-circle pictures so they make sense rather than get memorised.
  3. How to Prove It — VellemanYour first proof book: logic, quantifiers, sets, relations, functions and induction, then explicit proof strategies. Work the exercises; everything rigorous later on this path assumes it.
  4. Discrete Mathematics with Applications — Susanna EppThe discrete core computing builds on: counting, sequences, recursion, graphs and probability, with many worked examples. Skim the logic chapters Velleman already covered; pairs well with 6.042J if wanted.
  5. Calculus Made Easy — Silvanus P. ThompsonA warm, short first pass at derivatives and integrals. Read it in a few evenings to lose any fear of calculus before Stewart's Calculus, the next book on this path.
  6. Calculus — StewartYour main calculus text. Work the single-variable chapters now with plenty of exercises; return for the multivariable and vector-calculus chapters after Strang, later on this path.
  7. Introduction to Linear Algebra — StrangMatrices, elimination, vector spaces, eigenvalues and the SVD, with a computational, applied flavour. Then go back to Stewart's multivariable chapters. Pairs well with Strang's 18.06 lectures.
  8. Introduction to Probability — Blitzstein & HwangProbability as a way of reasoning, built from stories and strategies; uses single-variable calculus from Stewart. Work it chapter by chapter, doing the exercises.
  9. Probability and Statistics (4th ed.) — DeGroot & SchervishTurn probability into inference: estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, regression and Bayesian methods, each explained before it is proved. Builds directly on Blitzstein & Hwang.
  10. Regression and Other Stories — Gelman, Hill & VehtariApplied modelling: linear and logistic regression, simulation and causal inference from regression, fitted in R. The hands-on step after DeGroot & Schervish's theory.
  11. Ordinary Differential Equations — Tenenbaum & PollardLearn each ODE solution method through hundreds of fully worked examples; drill the linear-equation, oscillator and Laplace-transform lessons. Pairs well with 18.03 if wanted.
  12. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos — StrogatzThe geometric view of ODEs: phase portraits, stability, bifurcations, limit cycles and chaos through vivid applications. Uses Strang's eigenvalues and Tenenbaum & Pollard's methods.
  13. Linear Algebra Done Right — AxlerSecond pass at linear algebra: vector spaces and operators, proof-first. Now that Velleman and Strang are behind you, it trains the abstract style analysis and algebra need.
  14. Understanding Analysis — AbbottRigorous calculus: each chapter opens with the puzzle that makes rigour necessary. Work the exercises; it relies on Velleman's proof skills and Stewart's calculus.
  15. A Book of Abstract Algebra — PinterGroups, rings and fields in short, friendly chapters whose graded exercise sets make you build the theory yourself. Do the exercises — they are the book.

Where value diverges

Strang is the applied first course in linear algebra; Axler is the proofs-first second pass every future analyst or physicist needs. Calculus runs on Leonard and Stewart, then MIT 18.02, for fluency; Spivak is the rigorous detour, Abbott the rigorous destination. For proofs, Velleman builds the machinery and Cummings motivates; use both. Wasserman is the fast route through inference, Casella & Berger the deep one; McElreath teaches modelling and causal thinking neither covers. Videos build intuition but never replace working problems.

Physics

0 / 13 Essentials · 0 / 78

Reality from first principles. Requires the Mathematics essentials (calculus, linear algebra, differential equations). The core runs mechanics, E&M, thermal physics, quantum mechanics and relativity; astrophysics, condensed matter and particle physics are the electives.

Optimal path 12 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Big-picture orientationFirstThe Messenger Lectures — Richard Feynman (Cornell, 1964)MainThe Theoretical Minimum — SusskindPracticeThinking Physics — Lewis Carroll EpsteinRead the classical mechanics volume of Susskind first; watch a Feynman lecture when energy is low. Do two or three Epstein puzzles per session, committing to an answer before reading his.
  2. Introductory mechanicsFirstPhET Interactive Simulations — University of ColoradoMainUniversity Physics — Young & FreedmanPracticeMIT 8.01SC — Classical Mechanics — Deepto Chakrabarty, Peter Dourmashkin et al. (MIT)Play with the matching PhET simulation for ten minutes, then read Young & Freedman's mechanics chapters and work their examples. Use 8.01SC's worked-example videos and problem sets for practice. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  3. Introductory E&M and wavesFirstMath, Physics & Engineering Applets — Paul FalstadMainFundamentals of Physics II (PHYS 201) — Ramamurti Shankar (Yale)Watch one Shankar lecture per evening, then work the matching problems in Young & Freedman's electricity, magnetism and waves chapters. Open Falstad's field and wave applets to see what the equations describe.
  4. Vector calculus bridgeFirstVector Calculus and Partial Differential Equations — Steve BruntonMainDiv, Grad, Curl, and All That — H. M. ScheyAlsoMathematical Methods in the Physical Sciences — BoasWatch Brunton's short vector-calculus videos, then read Schey and do its problems. Keep Boas as your maths reference from here on: vector analysis now, Fourier series and ODEs when quantum needs them.
  5. Intermediate electromagnetismFirstA Student's Guide to Maxwell's Equations — FleischMainIntroduction to Electrodynamics — GriffithsWork Griffiths chapter by chapter, doing problems every session. When an equation feels opaque, read Fleisch's term-by-term walkthrough of it. Lean on Schey and Boas when the vector calculus bites.
  6. Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanicsFirstPhysics with Elliot — Elliot SchneiderMainClassical Mechanics — TaylorPracticeIntroduction to Classical Mechanics — MorinWatch Elliot's Lagrangian explainer first, then read Taylor and work its examples. Take a few Morin problems per week as stretch practice; his full solutions teach technique. Skip Taylor's chaos chapter if time is short.
  7. Thermal and statistical physicsMainAn Introduction to Thermal Physics — SchroederRead Schroeder in order, doing several problems per chapter. Revisit Young & Freedman's thermodynamics chapters first if they feel rusty.
  8. Quantum mechanicsMainIntroduction to Quantum Mechanics — GriffithsAlsoMIT 8.04 — Quantum Physics I — Barton Zwiebach (MIT)Read Griffiths and do its problems; watch the matching Zwiebach 8.04 lectures when a topic needs a second, slower explanation. Assumes linear algebra from the Mathematics path; use Boas for differential equations.
  9. Quantum formalism (optional)MainMIT 8.05 — Quantum Physics II — Barton Zwiebach (MIT)AlsoMastering Quantum Mechanics — Barton ZwiebachOptional second pass: 8.05's Dirac notation, spin and angular momentum, with Zwiebach's book for written derivations. Skip it if Griffiths felt solid and you want to reach relativity sooner.
  10. Special relativityMainSpacetime Physics — Taylor & WheelerAlsoMIT 8.20 — Introduction to Special Relativity — Markus Klute (MIT)Work Taylor & Wheeler's puzzles and draw spacetime diagrams by hand. Use Klute's short 8.20 lectures as a second voice on four-vectors and relativistic kinematics.
  11. General relativityMainGravity: An Introduction to Einstein's General Relativity — HartleHartle teaches the physics before the tensor machinery: orbits, light bending, black holes and gravitational waves. Do the problems; it builds directly on Taylor & Wheeler.
  12. Elective: condensed matterMainThe Oxford Solid State Basics — Steven H. SimonAlsoOxford Solid State Basics Lectures — Steven H. Simon (Oxford)Read Simon's short chapters and do the end-of-chapter problems; watch his matching Oxford lecture on low-energy evenings. Uses the quantum mechanics from Griffiths and the statistics from Schroeder.

Course path 12 steps
  1. CourseThe Theoretical Minimum lectures — Leonard Susskind (Stanford)BookThinking Physics — Lewis Carroll EpsteinBig-picture orientation: start with the classical mechanics lectures. Do two or three Epstein puzzles per session, committing to an answer first. Feynman’s Messenger Lectures make a good low-energy warm-up.
  2. CourseFundamentals of Physics I (PHYS 200) — Ramamurti Shankar (Yale)Newtonian mechanics, rotation, gravitation and oscillations; do the posted problem sets. Play with PhET simulations first; MIT 8.01SC’s worked examples are an alternative for extra drill.
  3. CourseFundamentals of Physics II (PHYS 201) — Ramamurti Shankar (Yale)Electricity, magnetism, waves and optics, one lecture per evening plus its problems. Open Falstad’s field and wave applets to see what the equations describe.
  4. CourseVector Calculus and Partial Differential Equations — Steve BruntonVector-calculus bridge: watch the divergence, curl and integral-theorem videos before intermediate electromagnetism. Return for its PDE videos when quantum mechanics needs them.
  5. CourseDavid Tong's Cambridge Lecture Notes — David TongRead Tong’s Electromagnetism notes, then Classical Dynamics for Lagrangians and Hamiltonians, working their problems. Physics with Elliot’s Lagrangian explainer is a good warm-up.
  6. BookIntroduction to Classical Mechanics — MorinStretch practice: a few Morin problems per week alongside Tong’s Classical Dynamics. Attempt each seriously before reading his full solutions, which teach technique.
  7. CourseMIT 8.333 — Statistical Mechanics — Mehran KardarThermal and statistical physics. The only full course here is graduate-level: one lecture over two evenings. If it is too steep, use Schroeder’s book from the Textbook path for this stage.
  8. CourseMIT 8.04 — Quantum Physics I — Barton Zwiebach (MIT)Wave mechanics, the harmonic oscillator, scattering and hydrogen. One lecture, then its problem set. Assumes linear algebra from the Mathematics path.
  9. CourseMIT 8.05 — Quantum Physics II — Barton Zwiebach (MIT)Optional second pass: Dirac notation, spin and angular momentum. Skip it if 8.04 felt solid and you want to reach relativity sooner.
  10. CourseMIT 8.20 — Introduction to Special Relativity — Markus Klute (MIT)Lorentz transformations, spacetime diagrams and four-vectors. Draw every spacetime diagram by hand and do the problem sets.
  11. CourseMIT 8.962 — General Relativity — Scott Hughes (MIT)Tensors, curvature, Einstein’s equations, black holes and gravitational waves. Graduate pace; A Thorough Introduction to General Relativity — Frederic Schuller is the geometry-first alternative.
  12. CourseOxford Solid State Basics Lectures — Steven H. Simon (Oxford)Elective: condensed matter, physics’s largest field. Crystals, phonons, bands, magnetism and semiconductors, using the quantum and statistical physics above.
Textbook path 11 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. The Theoretical Minimum — SusskindShort, conversational orientation: read the classical mechanics volume first to see the big picture before the full textbooks. Pairs well with Susskind's lectures if you want them.
  2. University Physics — Young & FreedmanYour first full pass through mechanics, E&M, waves, thermodynamics and modern physics. Work the worked examples and graded problems daily. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  3. Mathematical Methods in the Physical Sciences — BoasYour maths toolbox for everything after Young & Freedman. Learn each topic as later books need it: vector analysis first, then Fourier series and differential equations.
  4. Div, Grad, Curl, and All That — H. M. ScheyA short, gentle bridge into vector calculus through electrostatics. Read it just before Griffiths' electrodynamics, next on this path, so divergence and curl feel physical.
  5. Introduction to Electrodynamics — GriffithsIntermediate E&M, conversational and problem-driven. Work it chapter by chapter, doing the problems; lean on Schey and Boas when the vector calculus bites.
  6. Classical Mechanics — TaylorYour second, deeper pass on mechanics after Young & Freedman: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian methods, rotating frames, rigid bodies and chaos, with patient worked examples.
  7. An Introduction to Thermal Physics — SchroederEntropy from counting microstates, then engines, free energies, phase transitions and quantum statistics. Work its problems; it builds on the thermodynamics chapters of Young & Freedman.
  8. Introduction to Quantum Mechanics — GriffithsUndergraduate quantum mechanics: wave mechanics, formalism, hydrogen, spin and approximation methods. Do the problems; assumes linear algebra from the Mathematics path. Pairs well with MIT 8.04/8.05.
  9. Spacetime Physics — Taylor & WheelerSpecial relativity as spacetime geometry, taught through intuition and worked puzzles. Do it before any tensor machinery; it sets up Hartle, next on this path.
  10. Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein's General Relativity — HartleYour general relativity text, physics first: orbits, light bending, black holes and gravitational waves before the full formalism. Builds directly on Taylor & Wheeler.
  11. The Oxford Solid State Basics — Steven H. SimonFirst elective: condensed matter in short, clear chapters. Uses the quantum mechanics from Griffiths and the statistics from Schroeder; do the end-of-chapter problems.

Where value diverges

Feynman is peerless for intuition but a poor problem source, so pair it with Young & Freedman or Morin, and the Problem Solving group. Griffiths is the consensus teaching standard for E&M and QM; Sakurai and Jackson are the graduate upgrades. Shankar's Yale lectures and Zwiebach's MIT sequence are the guided spines. Lewin's famous demonstrations remain on YouTube but are no longer hosted by MIT, so they serve as a supplement rather than the main course.

Chemistry & Materials

0 / 5 Essentials · 0 / 34

Matter and transformation — the bridge from physics to life. Start with general chemistry, then organic and physical chemistry; inorganic chemistry and materials follow, with analytical chemistry as an elective; biochemistry lives in Biology. Physical chemistry assumes calculus.

Optimal path 7 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

Run ChemCollective titration, equilibrium and thermochemistry labs to test yourself.
  2. Organic chemistryFirstChad's Prep — Organic ChemistryMainOrganic Chemistry — KleinPracticeOrganic Chemistry as a Second Language — David KleinRead Klein and do every skill-builder. Watch Chad's Prep on a reaction class before or after reading it. Drill mechanisms in Second Language until arrow-pushing is reflex.
  3. Preview each topic with a TMP Chem video; use MIT 5.61's problem sets for practice. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  4. Thermodynamics and kineticsMainMolecular Driving Forces — Dill & BrombergAlsoMIT 5.60 — Thermodynamics & Kinetics — Keith Nelson & Moungi Bawendi (MIT)Build entropy and free energy from Dill & Bromberg, then work problems from McQuarrie & Simon's thermodynamics and kinetics chapters. Watch 5.60 lectures for kinetics and when a topic needs another explanation.
  5. Inorganic chemistryFirstPeriodic Videos — Brady Haran & Martyn PoliakoffMainInorganic Chemistry — Miessler, Fischer & TarrAlsoChem 107 — Inorganic Chemistry — Alan Heyduk (UC Irvine)Read Miessler on symmetry, MO bonding and coordination chemistry, doing problems.   6. Materials scienceFirstThe New Science of Strong Materials — J.E. Course path 8 steps
  1. CourseMIT 5.111SC — Principles of Chemical Science — Catherine Drennan (MIT)General chemistry: one lecture, then its problem set. Watch the matching Crash Course Chemistry episode first as a warm-up when a topic is new.
  2. CourseChemCollective Virtual Labs — Carnegie MellonTest yourself at the virtual bench: run the titration, equilibrium and thermochemistry labs and fix each misconception the feedback reveals.
  3. CourseOrganic Chemistry (Chem 51A–C) — James Nowick (UC Irvine)The organic lecture spine: structure, stereochemistry, mechanisms and synthesis, lecture by lecture. Draw every mechanism yourself as he does.
  4. CourseChad's Prep — Organic ChemistryBookOrganic Chemistry as a Second Language — David KleinAfter each Nowick lecture, do Chad’s lesson on the same reaction class, then drill Klein’s mechanism exercises until arrow-pushing is reflex.

Textbook path 7 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Chemistry: The Central Science — Brown, LeMay & BurstenYour general-chemistry foundation: atoms, bonding, stoichiometry, equilibria, acids and bases, thermochemistry. Read steadily and work the end-of-chapter problems; everything later builds on it.
  2. Organic Chemistry — KleinOrganic chemistry built for self-study. Work every skill-builder exercise and drill each mechanism until it is reflex; assumes bonding and acid-base chemistry from Brown.
  3. Physical Chemistry: A Molecular Approach — McQuarrie & SimonPhysical chemistry from quantum mechanics up, then thermodynamics and kinetics. Use its short maths-review chapters as needed; assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  4. Molecular Driving Forces — Dill & BrombergA second, clearer pass on statistical thermodynamics: entropy, free energy and equilibrium from first principles. Read it after McQuarrie & Simon's thermodynamics chapters to make them intuitive.
  5. Inorganic Chemistry — Miessler, Fischer & TarrSymmetry, molecular-orbital bonding, coordination chemistry and organometallics. Builds on the quantum chemistry in McQuarrie & Simon; do the problem sets.
  6. Materials Science and Engineering — CallisterFrom bonds to real materials: crystal structure, defects, phase diagrams, mechanical behaviour, metals, ceramics and polymers. Work the example problems in each chapter.
  7. Quantitative Chemical Analysis — Harris & LucyElective: measurement and analysis — error analysis, equilibria, titrations, electrochemistry, spectrophotometry and chromatography. Builds on Brown's equilibrium chapters; its worked examples are exceptionally clear.

Earth, Climate & Environment

0 / 2 Essentials · 0 / 24

The planet as a physical system — energy balance, carbon, oceans and atmosphere, deep time. The quantitative layer beneath every climate argument you will hear. Requires basic physics and chemistry.

Optimal path 8 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Energy numeracyMainSustainable Energy: Without the Hot Air — David MacKayPracticeOur World in DataRead MacKay in short chunks, redoing his arithmetic yourself. MacKay's data is from 2008, so check each key number against current Our World in Data charts and note what changed.
  2. Climate physicsMainGlobal Warming I: The Science and Modeling of Climate Change — David Archer (UChicago)AlsoGlobal Warming: Understanding the Forecast — David ArcherPracticeClimate Interactive Models — UChicago (forecast.uchicago.edu)Watch Archer's lectures, then run the matching model yourself and change one lever at a time. Read the matching book chapter when you want the working written out.

  4. The Earth systemFirstA Brief History of Earth — Andrew KnollMainThe Earth System — Kump, Kasting & CraneRead Knoll's short narrative first for the four-billion-year story, then Kump for the carbon cycle, feedbacks and coupled atmosphere, ocean, biosphere and rock.
  5. PaleoclimateMainEarth's Climate: Past and Future — William RuddimanIce ages, orbital cycles and past greenhouse worlds: the record that tests today's climate models. Builds directly on Kump.

(MIT)The rigorous follow-up to MacKay: pick the chapters on the technologies you care about. Use 22.081J's problem sets to practise comparing energy options quantitatively.

Textbook path 7 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Sustainable Energy: Without the Hot Air — David MacKayStart here: every energy option in the same units, so you can judge any plan by arithmetic. Read it straight through; it is free online.
  2. Global Warming: Understanding the Forecast — David ArcherCore climate physics with algebra only: radiation, the greenhouse layer model, the carbon cycle and feedbacks. Read chapter by chapter and run the online models it uses.
  3. The Earth System — Kump, Kasting & CraneAtmosphere, ocean, biosphere and rock as one coupled system: carbon cycle, feedbacks and Earth's history. Widens Archer's climate picture to the whole planet.
  4. Earth's Climate: Past and Future — William RuddimanThe paleoclimate record: ice ages, orbital cycles and past greenhouse worlds. Read after Kump to see how Earth's past calibrates the models.
  5. Global Physical Climatology — Dennis HartmannThe quantitative step up from Archer: radiation, energy balance, the hydrologic cycle, circulation and climate sensitivity. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path; work the exercises.
  6. Atmosphere, Ocean and Climate Dynamics — John Marshall & R. Alan PlumbThe fluid dynamics of air and sea: convection, Coriolis, geostrophy, jets and ocean circulation. Builds on Hartmann; assumes calculus and introductory mechanics from the Physics path.
  7. The Physics of Energy — Robert Jaffe & Washington TaylorThe rigorous follow-up to MacKay: the physics of combustion, nuclear, solar, wind and storage. Pick chapters by interest; assumes introductory physics from the Physics path.

Where value diverges

Archer is the entry point and the one to work properly; Hartmann is the next step and Pierrehumbert the rigor upgrade once you can derive the layer model. MacKay is not a climate book but an arithmetic book, the fastest cure for innumeracy about energy, so read it early. Ruddiman supplies the deep-time record that makes the models credible; Marshall & Plumb add the fluid dynamics of ocean and air.

Biology & Life Sciences

0 / 10 Essentials · 0 / 55

Life from molecules to ecosystems: a core of introductory biology, biochemistry, cell biology, genetics and evolution, then electives in physiology, neuroscience, immunology, ecology, development and computational biology. Medicine now has its own subject. Prerequisite: general chemistry before biochemistry and cell biology.

Course path 10 steps
  1. CourseMIT 7.012 — Introductory Biology — Lander et al. (MIT)The logic of modern biology: biochemistry, genetics and molecular biology. Watch Amoeba Sisters on a topic first for quick intuition, then Lander’s lecture and problem set.
  2. CourseMIT 7.05 — General Biochemistry — Michael Yaffe & Matthew Vander Heiden (MIT)BookThe Vital Question — Nick LaneProteins, enzymes and metabolism; do the problems. After the metabolism lectures, read Lane on how proton gradients shaped life’s origin.
  3. CourseMIT 7.06x — Cell Biology — Lamason, Cheeseman & Lourido (MITx)BookThe Machinery of Life — David S. GoodsellTransport, signalling, cytoskeleton and cell cycle, taught through experiments. Browse Goodsell’s paintings to picture the crowded cell.
  4. CourseMIT 7.03x — Genetics — Hemann, Reddien, Gehring & Corradin (MITx)Genetics is learned by solving problems: watch each lecture, then do its problem set, from Mendelian analysis through to population genetics.
  5. CoursePrinciples of Evolution, Ecology and Behavior (EEB 122) — Stephen Stearns (Yale)BookThe Selfish Gene — DawkinsEvolution first (selection, drift, speciation, phylogenies), then life history, populations, communities and behaviour. Read Dawkins alongside for the gene’s-eye view.
  6. CourseNinja NerdPhysiology: work through the organ systems on the whiteboard with him, then draw each homeostatic feedback loop from memory.
  7. CourseFundamentals of Neuroscience — David Cox (HarvardX)The neuron’s electrical properties, neurons and networks, and the brain, with animations and simulations. Do each module’s exercises.
  8. CourseMIT 9.13 — The Human Brain — Nancy KanwisherBookThe Spike — Mark HumphriesHow the brain implements vision, faces, language and thought. Read Humphries alongside for an accurate picture of how neurons compute.
  9. CourseImmunology with Hematology (BioSci M121) — Walsh & Fruman (UC Irvine)Elective: innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, T cells and blood. Draw the sequence of an immune response after each lecture.
  10. CourseSystems Biology — Uri Alon (Weizmann)Quantitative capstone: network motifs, robustness and optimal design in cells. Do the exercises. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
Textbook path 10 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Campbell Biology — Urry et al.Your foundation: every area of biology at introductory level. Read it through, using the figures and review questions; later books go deeper on each part.
  2. Biochemistry: A Short Course — Tymoczko, Berg, Gatto & StryerProteins, enzymes and metabolism in short, focused chapters with clinical examples. Assumes general chemistry from the Chemistry path; builds on Campbell's chemistry-of-life chapters.
  3. Essential Cell Biology — Alberts et al.The clearest cell biology text: membranes, transport, signalling, cytoskeleton and the cell cycle. Read after Tymoczko's biochemistry; use its end-of-chapter questions.
  4. An Introduction to Genetic Analysis — Griffiths et al.Genetic reasoning through problems: Mendelian and molecular genetics, mapping and population genetics. Work its problem sets; pairs well with MIT 7.03x if you want lectures.
  5. Evolution: Making Sense of Life — Zimmer & EmlenEvolution taught through vivid examples: selection, drift, speciation, phylogenetics and human evolution. Builds on the population genetics in Griffiths' genetic analysis.
  6. Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach — SilverthornHow organ systems maintain homeostasis, from cells up: cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, digestive. Builds on Essential Cell Biology; read system by system.
  7. Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain — Bear, Connors & ParadisoFrom neurons and synapses to senses, movement, memory and emotion, with excellent figures. Builds on Silverthorn's nervous-system chapters; read part by part.
  8. Ecology: Concepts and Applications — Anna Sher & Manuel MollesPopulations, communities and ecosystems, with the field studies behind them. Builds on Zimmer & Emlen's evolutionary thinking; a clear, example-rich read.
  9. How the Immune System Works — Lauren SompayracElective: a short, conversational tour of the whole immune system. Read it straight through; a natural bridge to the Medicine path.
  10. An Introduction to Systems Biology — AlonQuantitative capstone: design principles of gene circuits and network motifs. Do the exercises; assumes differential equations from the Mathematics path. Pairs well with Alon's lectures.

Where value diverges

After the core (Campbell, biochemistry, cell biology, genetics and evolution), paths split by goal. Medicine-bound learners go Physiology, then Immunology & Microbiology, then the Medicine & Health subject. Quantitative and programming-minded learners go to Systems & Computational and the Neuromatch notebooks. Naturalists go to Ecology & Behavior and Developmental Biology. Molecular Biology of the Cell and Kandel are references to return to, not books to finish.

Medicine & Health

0 / 3 Essentials · 0 / 9

How the body fails and how medicine responds — anatomy, mechanisms of disease, drugs, and the evidence behind clinical claims. Assumes the Biology core, especially Physiology and Immunology.

Optimal path 5 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Reading medical evidenceMainHow to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare — Trisha GreenhalghRead first: short, friendly chapters on trial designs, reviews and screening. After each chapter, pick a health headline and judge the study behind it.
  2. AnatomyMainKenhubAlsoAtlas of Human Anatomy — Frank H. NetterDo a Kenhub lesson and its spaced-repetition quiz each session, region by region. Open the matching Netter plate to fix 3D relationships. Assumes physiology from the Biology path.
  3. Mechanisms of diseaseMainPathoma — Husain SattarAlsoRobbins & Kumar Basic Pathology — Kumar, Abbas & AsterWatch a Pathoma chapter and read its companion book: cell injury, inflammation and neoplasia first, then organ systems. Read the matching Robbins chapter afterwards for depth.
  4. PharmacologyMainLippincott Illustrated Reviews: Pharmacology — Whalen et al.AlsoRang & Dale's Pharmacology — Ritter et al.Learn drug classes from Lippincott's diagrams and summary tables, answering its study questions. Optional: read Rang & Dale for receptors, dose-response and pharmacokinetics in more depth.
  5. EpidemiologyMainGordis Epidemiology (7th ed.) — David Celentano, Moyses Szklo & Youssef FaragThe systematic follow-up to Greenhalgh: study designs, bias, confounding, screening and causation. Work the review questions at the end of each chapter.
Course path 3 steps
  1. CourseKenhubBookAtlas of Human Anatomy — Frank H. NetterAnatomy region by region: a Kenhub lesson and its spaced-repetition quiz each session, with the matching Netter plate open. Assumes physiology from the Biology path.
  2. CoursePathoma — Husain SattarMechanisms of disease: watch each chapter with its companion book, starting with cell injury, inflammation and neoplasia, then the organ systems.
  3. BookHallmarks of Cancer: The Next Generation — Hanahan & WeinbergAfter Pathoma’s neoplasia chapter, read this landmark review to organise cancer biology as a small set of acquired capabilities.
Textbook path 5 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare — Trisha GreenhalghRead first: a short, friendly guide to judging medical evidence — trial designs, reviews, screening, sensitivity and specificity. It changes how you read everything after.
  2. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology — Kumar, Abbas & AsterThe core of this path: how disease happens — cell injury, inflammation, neoplasia, then organ systems. Assumes physiology from the Biology path; pairs well with Pathoma's videos.
  3. Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Pharmacology — Whalen et al.Your first pass on drugs: classes, mechanisms, side effects and interactions in diagrams and tables. Read after Robbins' general pathology chapters; use the review questions.
  4. Rang & Dale's Pharmacology — Ritter et al.Optional deeper pass after Lippincott: receptors, dose-response, pharmacokinetics and toxicity explained from mechanism. Read the general-principles chapters, then drug classes by interest.
  5. Gordis Epidemiology (7th ed.) — David Celentano, Moyses Szklo & Youssef FaragThe systematic follow-up to Greenhalgh: study designs, bias, confounding, screening and causation, clearly explained. Work the chapter review questions.

Where value diverges

Medical students converge on short, visual, mechanism-first resources (Pathoma, Lippincott, Kenhub) for learning, and keep the big textbooks (Robbins, Rang & Dale, Netter) as references. Epidemiology is the piece most self-learners skip and most need: it is what lets you judge any health claim you will ever read.

Computer Science

0 / 23 Essentials · 0 / 116

The core spine of a computer science degree — programming, algorithms, machines, operating systems, concurrency, networks, databases, languages, theory and security. Pair the early groups with discrete maths from Mathematics; applied craft lives in Software Engineering and distributed systems in System Design.

Optimal path 17 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Programming from zeroFirstCrash Course Computer Science — Carrie Anne PhilbinMainCS50 — David Malan (Harvard)Watch a few Crash Course episodes for the big map, then work CS50 week by week. Do every problem set; they are the learning, the lectures are the setup.
  2. Shell, Git and toolsFirstWizard Zines — Julia EvansMainThe Missing Semester — MITPracticeLearn Git Branching — Peter CottleOne Missing Semester lecture per session, typing along. Do Learn Git Branching's levels after the Git lecture; read a Wizard Zine whenever a tool feels opaque.
  3. Abstraction and recursionMainComposing Programs — John DeNero (Berkeley)PracticeAdvent of Code — Eric WastlRead Composing Programs in short sections and do every exercise; chapter 3's interpreter is the payoff. Use old Advent of Code puzzles as low-stakes weekend practice.
  4. Algorithms and data structuresFirstVisuAlgoMainAlgorithms Illuminated — RoughgardenPracticeCSES Problem SetAssumes discrete maths and proofs from the Mathematics path. Watch each structure run in VisuAlgo first, read Roughgarden's chapter, then solve two or three matching CSES problems.
  5. A computer from gatesFirstCode — Charles PetzoldMainNand2Tetris — Nisan & SchockenRead Code for the story of how relays become a CPU, then build it yourself in Nand2Tetris. Each project is a satisfying, testable win; the hardware half alone is worthwhile.
  6. C and the machineMainDive into Systems — Matthews, Newhall & WebbYour gentle systems text: C, data representation, assembly, caches. Read a section per session and do its exercises; it teaches all the C the rest of this path assumes.
  7. Systems, second passMainComputer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective — Bryant & O'HallaronPracticeCMU 15-213 (CS:APP) — Bryant & O'HallaronOptional depth after Dive into Systems. Skip chapter 4 (processor design) at first. The 15-213 Bomb and Malloc labs are where it sticks; do them over the reading.
  8. Operating systemsFirstCore DumpedMainOperating Systems: Three Easy Pieces — Arpaci-Dusseau & Arpaci-DusseauPracticeMIT 6.1810 — Operating System Engineering (xv6) — MITWatch the matching Core Dumped video, read the short OSTEP chapter, run its homework simulators. Add the 6.1810 xv6 labs once virtualization and concurrency make sense.
  9. Concurrency and locksFirstThe Deadlock EmpireMainRust Atomics and Locks — Mara BosPlay The Deadlock Empire first to feel races and deadlocks. Then Bos: atomics, memory ordering, and building your own locks and channels; needs basic Rust syntax.
  10. Computer networkingMainComputer Networking: A Top-Down Approach — Kurose & RossPracticeBeej's Guide to Network Programming — BeejKurose & Ross chapters 1–6 are the core; do the Wireshark labs. When you reach the transport layer, write a small socket client and server with Beej's Guide.
  11. Database internalsMainCMU 15-445 — Database Systems — Andy PavloPracticeSQLBoltIf SQL is rusty, do SQLBolt in an evening first. Then Pavlo's 15-445 lectures, the clearest teaching on storage, indexes and transactions; attempt the projects if you want depth.
  12. Languages and interpretersMainCrafting Interpreters — NystromAlsoProgramming Languages A/B/C — Dan Grossman (UW)Type along with Crafting Interpreters, tree-walker first, then the bytecode VM. Grossman's Part A is the companion for language ideas: closures, pattern matching, static types.
  13. Build it yourselfMainCodeCraftersAlsobuild-your-own-xRebuild real tools from scratch: start with CodeCrafters' shell or Redis challenge, whose tests tell you when each step works. For free alternatives, pick one build-your-own-x tutorial and finish it.
  14. Theory of computationMainIntroduction to the Theory of Computation — SipserAlsoMIT 18.404 — Theory of Computation — Michael Sipser (MIT)Assumes proof comfort from the Mathematics path. Read Sipser's book and do exercises; when a proof doesn't click, watch his matching 18.404 lecture for the intuition.
  15. Applied cryptographyMainSerious Cryptography (2nd ed.) — Jean-Philippe AumassonPracticeCryptoHackAssumes modular arithmetic from the Mathematics path. Read a Serious Cryptography chapter, then do the matching CryptoHack challenges; the gamified levels keep momentum.
  16. Security engineeringFirstReflections on Trusting Trust — Ken ThompsonMainComputer Security — Wagner, Weaver, Kao et al. (UC Berkeley CS 161)Practicepwn.college — Yan Shoshitaishvili (ASU)Start with Thompson's three pages. Read the CS 161 text; its memory-safety part builds on Dive into Systems. Practise in pwn.college, starting with the beginner dojos.
  17. Information theoryMainInformation Theory: A Tutorial Introduction — James V. StoneAlsoInformation Theory, Pattern Recognition and Neural Networks — David MacKay (Cambridge)PracticeInformation Theory, Inference & Learning Algorithms — MacKayAssumes basic probability from the Mathematics path. Stone first, with worked examples. Then MacKay's lectures, working the exercises in his book alongside them.
Then, by interest
  • Quantum Computing — start with Understanding Quantum Information and Computation — John Watrous (IBM Quantum)

Course path 16 steps
  1. CourseCS50 — David Malan (Harvard)Watch a few Crash Course Computer Science episodes first as a warm-up map. Then work CS50 week by week, doing every problem set yourself.
  2. CourseThe Missing Semester — MITBookWizard Zines — Julia EvansOne lecture per session, typing along: shell, Git, editors, debugging. Read the matching Wizard Zines; Learn Git Branching is an optional alternative drill for branching.
  3. CourseBerkeley CS61A / 61B / 61C — UC BerkeleyTake 61A for abstraction, recursion, higher-order functions and interpreters. 61B and 61C are optional depth; Advent of Code is an alternative source of practice puzzles.

One lecture at a time; step through it in VisuAlgo if unclear. Then practise the Handbook's techniques; CSES Problem Set is its judged practice alternative.
  5. CourseNand2Tetris — Nisan & SchockenBookCode — Charles PetzoldRead Code for how relays become a CPU, then build it yourself in Nand2Tetris: gates, ALU, CPU, assembler, VM, compiler.
  6. CourseCMU 15-213 (CS:APP) — Bryant & O'HallaronC, data representation, assembly, memory and caches. Watch the lectures and do the Bomb, Attack and Malloc labs.
  7. CourseMIT 6.1810 — Operating System Engineering (xv6) — MITWatch Core Dumped videos first as a warm-up on processes and virtual memory. Then do the xv6 kernel labs; Berkeley CS 162 is the lecture-first alternative.
  8. CourseStanford CS149 — Parallel Computing — Kayvon Fatahalian & Kunle Olukotun (Stanford)BookThe Little Book of Semaphores — Allen DowneyPlay The Deadlock Empire first as a warm-up. Then CS149 for multicore, SIMD, GPUs and locks; solve Downey's synchronisation puzzles alongside.
  9. CourseStanford CS144 — Computer Networking — Keith Winstein (Stanford)Networks layer by layer, building TCP piece by piece in the labs. Hussein Nasser's Fundamentals of Networking is the gentler, lecture-only alternative.
  10. CourseCMU 15-445 — Database Systems — Andy PavloBookArchitecture of a Database System — Hellerstein, Stonebraker & HamiltonIf SQL is rusty, do SQLBolt first as a warm-up. Then Pavlo's lectures on storage, indexes, execution and transactions; read Hellerstein alongside.
  11. CourseProgramming Languages A/B/C — Dan Grossman (UW)What languages are made of: closures, types, pattern matching, dynamic versus static typing. Do every homework, including the small interpreter.
  12. CourseCodeCraftersRebuild real tools from scratch, starting with the shell or Redis challenge; its tests tell you when each step works. build-your-own-x is the free alternative.
  13. CourseMIT 18.404 — Theory of Computation — Michael Sipser (MIT)Assumes proof comfort from the Mathematics path. Automata, computability and complexity; attempt each proof before Sipser finishes it.
  14. CourseCryptography I — Dan Boneh (Stanford)Assumes modular arithmetic. Watch a week of Boneh, then the matching CryptoHack challenges are the hands-on alternative for making it concrete.
  15. Coursepwn.college — Yan Shoshitaishvili (ASU)BookReflections on Trusting Trust — Ken ThompsonRead Thompson's three pages first. Then work pwn.college's dojos belt by belt; picoCTF is the gentler warm-up if it feels steep.
  16. CourseInformation Theory, Pattern Recognition and Neural Networks — David MacKay (Cambridge)BookA Mathematical Theory of Communication — Claude ShannonMacKay's lectures on entropy, source coding and noisy channels; then read Shannon's founding paper, now readable with the lectures behind you.
Textbook path 15 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Composing Programs — John DeNero (Berkeley)Your programming foundation in Python: functions, data abstraction, recursion and building an interpreter. Work every chapter's exercises; pairs well with CS61A if you want lectures.
  2. Pro Git — Scott Chacon & Ben StraubRead chapters 1–3 (basics and branching) now; dip into later chapters as needs arise, and chapter 10 when you want Git's internals.
  3. Algorithms Illuminated — RoughgardenYour algorithms text: sorting, graphs, hashing, greedy, dynamic programming, NP-hardness, with worked examples. Assumes discrete maths and proofs from the Mathematics path; do the problems.
  4. Dive into Systems — Matthews, Newhall & WebbYour first systems book: C, data representation, assembly, caches, the OS and parallelism, gently paced. It teaches the C the rest of this path assumes.
  5. Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective — Bryant & O'HallaronThe deeper second pass after Dive into Systems: machine code, linking, memory hierarchy, exceptions, virtual memory. Skip chapter 4 (processor design) at first; 15-213 labs pair well.
  6. Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces — Arpaci-Dusseau & Arpaci-DusseauBuilds on Dive into Systems and CS:APP: virtualization, concurrency, persistence in short chapters. Run the homework simulators; 6.1810's xv6 labs pair well if you want them.
  7. Rust Atomics and Locks — Mara BosAfter OSTEP's concurrency part: atomics, memory ordering, and building your own spin locks, channels and mutexes. Needs basic Rust syntax; the ideas carry to C++.
  8. Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach — Kurose & RossNetworks from HTTP and DNS down through TCP, routing and link layers. The first six chapters are the core; do the Wireshark labs.
  9. Database System Concepts — Silberschatz et al.Your databases text: the relational model, SQL, storage, indexing, query processing, transactions and recovery. Read the core chapters; pairs well with CMU 15-445 if you want lectures.
  10. Crafting Interpreters — NystromExtends Composing Programs' interpreter: build a tree-walker in Java, then a bytecode VM in C. Type along with every chapter and do the challenges you enjoy.
  11. Introduction to the Theory of Computation — SipserAutomata, computability and complexity, with proofs that read like explanations. Assumes proof comfort from the Mathematics path; do the exercises.
  12. Serious Cryptography (2nd ed.) — Jean-Philippe AumassonA practical tour of modern cryptography: randomness, ciphers, AEAD, hashing, RSA, elliptic curves, TLS, post-quantum. Assumes modular arithmetic from the Mathematics path.
  13. Computer Security — Wagner, Weaver, Kao et al. (UC Berkeley CS 161)Security principles, memory-safety attacks (CS:APP's machine-level chapters prepare you), applied crypto, web and network security. pwn.college dojos make good optional practice afterwards.
  14. Information Theory: A Tutorial Introduction — James V. StoneGentle first pass: entropy, mutual information and channel capacity built up with worked examples. Assumes basic probability from the Mathematics path.
  15. Information Theory, Inference & Learning Algorithms — MacKayThe deeper step after Stone: compression, noisy-channel coding and Bayesian inference. Do the exercises; MacKay's Cambridge lectures pair well.

Where value diverges

Learn algorithms from Roughgarden alongside MIT 6.1210, and keep CLRS as the comprehensive reference; Erickson is the free alternative and Skiena teaches choosing an algorithm. For compilers, Crafting Interpreters first, then Engineering a Compiler — the Dragon Book is dated. Software Engineering: Code to Production

0 / 11 Essentials · 0 / 61

How to build software that stays easy to change and runs well: code design, testing, refactoring, architecture inside and between services, delivery, reliability, performance and containers. Start after the CS foundations. Where this stops: scaling, data and distribution across many machines live in System Design.

Optimal path 14 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Professional engineering habitsMainThe Pragmatic Programmer — Thomas & HuntYour gentle start: short independent sections, one per evening. After each, note one habit to try at work this week.
  2. Managing complexityFirstArjanCodes — Arjan EggesMainA Philosophy of Software Design — OusterhoutRead a chapter, then hunt its red flags in code your team owns. Use ArjanCodes videos when you want to see a design critiqued and refactored on screen.
  3. Specs, tests and ADTsMainMIT 6.102 — Software Construction — MITAlsoParse, Don't Validate — Alexis KingDo the readings with their exercises and the problem sets, not just the notes. Read Parse, Don't Validate alongside the ADT material. Assumes programming from the Computer Science path.
  4. Tests worth writingMainUnit Testing: Principles, Practices, and Patterns — Vladimir KhorikovPracticeTest-Driven Development by Example — Kent BeckRead Khorikov for which tests pay off, then type along with Beck's worked examples to feel the red-green-refactor rhythm on a small kata.
  5. Refactoring and legacy codeMainRefactoring — Martin FowlerAlsoWorking Effectively with Legacy Code — Michael FeathersWork through Fowler's opening example and code-smells chapter; keep the catalogue as reference. Reach for Feathers when the code you must change has no tests.
  6. Architecture fundamentalsFirstSoftware Architecture Monday — Mark RichardsMainFundamentals of Software Architecture (2nd ed.) — Richards & FordRead the book cover to cover; it frames everything after it. Watch a short Software Architecture Monday lesson on a topic first when a chapter feels abstract.
  7. Domain boundariesMainLearning Domain-Driven Design — Vlad KhononovPracticeArchitecture Patterns with Python — Harry Percival & Bob GregoryRead Khononov to decide where boundaries fall, then build Architecture Patterns with Python's example step by step with its tests to make the patterns concrete.
  8. Services and boundariesMainBuilding Microservices (2nd ed.) — Sam NewmanAlsoSoftware Architecture: The Hard Parts — Ford, Richards, Sadalage & DehghaniRead Newman for when and how to split a system into services. Dip into The Hard Parts for the trade-off decisions. Scaling and data across services continue in System Design, which teaches DDIA.
  9. What drives deliveryFirstThe Phoenix Project — Kim, Behr & SpaffordMainAccelerate — Forsgren, Humble & KimAlsoModern Software Engineering channel — Dave FarleyOptionally start with The Phoenix Project as an easy story. Read Accelerate's findings closely; skim the statistics part. Farley's short videos explain individual practices.
  10. Engineering at scaleMainSoftware Engineering at Google — Winters, Manshreck & WrightAlsoTeam Topologies — Matthew Skelton & Manuel PaisPick chapters by your team's current pain points. Read Team Topologies for how team structure shapes architecture, which matters directly in your manager role.
  11. Reliability and SLOsMainSite Reliability Engineering — GoogleAlsoRelease It! — NygardPracticeThe Site Reliability Workbook — GoogleRead the SLO, error-budget, toil, monitoring, on-call and postmortem chapters; skip the rest. Draft SLOs for one service with the Workbook. Release It! adds stability patterns.

Observability and tracingFirstUsing Canonical Log Lines for Online Visibility — Brandur LeachMainObservability Engineering — Majors, Fong-Jones & MirandaPracticeOpenTelemetry Documentation — OpenTelemetryRead the short canonical-log-lines essay first, then the book. Practise by instrumenting a small service with OpenTelemetry and tracing one request end to end.

Read Gregg's methodology chapters closely and use the rest as reference. The MIT course is optional depth for code-level optimisation. Assumes operating systems from the Computer Science path.

Course path 10 steps
  1. CourseArjanCodes — Arjan EggesManaging complexity by example: watch a design critiqued and refactored on screen, then hunt the same smell in code your team owns.
  2. CourseMIT 6.102 — Software Construction — MITBookParse, Don't Validate — Alexis KingSpecs, tests, ADTs, immutability. Do the readings' exercises and problem sets; read King's essay alongside the ADT material. Assumes programming from Computer Science.
  3. CourseDesign Patterns — Christopher OkhraviNow that 6.102 has given you interfaces, watch one pattern per evening and sketch where it would help, or hurt, in your codebase.
  4. CourseSoftware Architecture Fundamentals — Mark Richards & Neal FordArchitecture styles and trade-off analysis. When a topic feels abstract, watch a short Software Architecture Monday lesson on it as a warm-up.
  5. CourseModern Software Engineering channel — Dave FarleyBookThe Phoenix Project — Kim, Behr & SpaffordWhat drives delivery: read The Phoenix Project as an easy story of flow and bottlenecks, then Farley's one-concept videos on continuous delivery and TDD.
  6. CourseSadServersReliability by doing: fix a genuinely broken Linux server against a scripted check, one scenario per evening, noting your debugging steps afterwards.
  7. CourseOpenTelemetry Documentation — OpenTelemetryBookUsing Canonical Log Lines for Online Visibility — Brandur LeachRead the canonical-log-lines essay first. Then the OpenTelemetry concepts; instrument a small service and trace one request end to end.
  8. CourseMIT 6.1060 (OCW: 6.172) — Performance Engineering of Software Systems — Leiserson & Shun (MIT)Watch Gil Tene's How NOT to Measure Latency first as a warm-up. Then the MIT lectures for measurement-driven, code-level optimisation.
  9. CourseKubernetes Concepts — kubernetes.ioWatch Liz Rice's Containers From Scratch first as a warm-up. Then read the Concepts pages: pods, controllers, the reconciliation loop, on a local cluster.
  10. Courseiximiuz Labs — Ivan VelichkoPractise each container and Kubernetes concept in browser playgrounds; do the challenge after reading its tutorial.
Textbook path 13 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. The Pragmatic Programmer — Thomas & HuntStart here: the habits of a professional engineer — orthogonality, tracer bullets, automation, ownership. Short independent sections, ideal for one per evening.
  2. A Philosophy of Software Design — OusterhoutThe core design text: deep modules, information hiding, comments as design. Short; after each chapter, look for its red flags in code you manage.
  3. Unit Testing: Principles, Practices, and Patterns — Vladimir KhorikovWhich tests are worth writing — the four pillars of a good test, mocks versus real collaborators. Read before you set testing standards for a team.
  4. Refactoring — Martin FowlerRead the opening worked example and the code-smells chapter, then use the catalogue as a reference; it relies on the tests Khorikov taught you to write.
  5. Fundamentals of Software Architecture (2nd ed.) — Richards & FordArchitecture as a discipline — characteristics, modularity, styles from layered to microservices, trade-off analysis. Read cover to cover; it frames everything after it.
  6. Learning Domain-Driven Design — Vlad KhononovA clear on-ramp to DDD — bounded contexts, aggregates, context mapping. Use it to decide where module and service boundaries should fall.
  7. Building Microservices (2nd ed.) — Sam NewmanService-based architecture: finding boundaries, splitting a monolith step by step, integration and data ownership. Read after Khononov; for scaling and data across services, go on to System Design.
  8. Accelerate — Forsgren, Humble & KimThe research on which practices predict delivery performance and the DORA metrics. Short; read the findings closely and skim the statistical-method part.
  9. Software Engineering at Google — Winters, Manshreck & WrightEngineering as programming over time — code review, testing at scale, dependencies, builds, deprecation. Pick chapters by your team's current pain points.
  10. Site Reliability Engineering — GoogleAn essay collection: read the SLO, error-budget, toil, monitoring, on-call and postmortem chapters first; skip the rest freely.
  11. Observability Engineering — Majors, Fong-Jones & MirandaBuilds on the SRE book's SLOs: structured events, high-cardinality data, tracing and SLO-based alerting for debugging systems you didn't predict.
  12. Systems Performance — Brendan GreggRead the methodology chapters (USE method, flame graphs, tracing) closely; keep the rest as reference. Assumes operating-systems basics from the Computer Science path.
  13. Kubernetes: Up and Running — Burns, Beda & HightowerContainers and orchestration from Kubernetes' creators — what problem it solves and why it is shaped that way. Follow along on a local cluster.
