Where value diverges

For code quality, A Philosophy of Software Design and MIT 6.102 teach the thinking, The Pragmatic Programmer the habits; Refactoring and the testing books are the working toolkit. Fundamentals of Software Architecture covers styles and trade-offs; Building Microservices and The Hard Parts cover when and how to split. Accelerate is the evidence base for delivery, and the Google SRE book defines reliability's vocabulary. Performance splits into whole-system methodology (Gregg) and CPU-level optimisation (Bakhvalov, Muratori).

Web Development

0 / 6 Essentials · 0 / 40

The practical craft of building for the web. Run one full-stack path end to end (The Odin Project is the default), using the topic groups — HTML, CSS and accessibility, JavaScript, TypeScript, React and frameworks, browser and performance, testing and tooling — alongside and after it for depth. Server-side depth continues in Backend Engineering.

Optimal path 12 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  2. JavaScript properlyMainJavaScript.infoAlsoTasks, microtasks, queues and schedules — Jake ArchibaldPracticeJavaScript30 — Wes BosRead JavaScript.info alongside Odin, doing its tasks. Build a JavaScript30 project per session. Use Archibald's interactive article when you reach the event loop.
  3. A mental model of CSSFirstKevin Powell — CSSMainCSS for JavaScript Developers — Josh ComeauPracticeFrontend MentorComeau's interactive course replaces CSS trial and error with understanding. Watch Kevin Powell for any single feature that's fuzzy. Build a Frontend Mentor challenge per module.
  4. Visual design and layoutMainRefactoring UI — Adam Wathan & Steve SchogerAlsoEvery Layout — Heydon Pickering & Andy BellRefactoring UI's before-and-after rules are quick wins; apply one to an old Frontend Mentor build. Every Layout then teaches intrinsic layouts that adapt without breakpoints.
  5. Web accessibilityMainPractical Accessibility — Sara SoueidanAlsoInclusive Components — Heydon PickeringWork through Soueidan's course, testing your own pages with a screen reader. Use Inclusive Components as the pattern book for toggles, menus and tabs.

  7. Full-stack rigourMainFull Stack Open — University of HelsinkiThe rigorous modern-stack course: React, Node, testing, a database. Do the exercises and submit them; skip or skim parts you already covered in Odin.
  8. TypeScript by defaultMainTotal TypeScript — Matt PocockAlsoEffective TypeScript (2nd ed.) — Dan VanderkamPracticeType Challenges — Anthony FuWork Total TypeScript's exercise-driven Essentials. Do warm-up and easy Type Challenges for generics practice. Read Effective TypeScript's items afterwards to learn to think in types.
  9. Server-rendered ReactMainLearn Next.js — VercelAlsoPatterns.dev — Lydia Hallie & Addy OsmaniBuild Vercel's dashboard app: Server Components, streaming, Server Actions. Read Patterns.dev's rendering patterns to understand why each choice exists.
  10. Browser and performanceFirstInside look at modern web browser — Mariko KosakaMainweb.dev — GoogleKosaka's four illustrated parts first, to see the rendering pipeline. Then web.dev's Learn performance material and Core Web Vitals; measure your Next.js app as you go.
  11. Testing and qualityMainEpic Web — Kent C. DoddsAlsoPlaywright Documentation — MicrosoftDo Epic Web's testing workshops with Vitest. Then add Playwright end-to-end tests to your Next.js app, using its docs for locators, auto-waiting and tracing.
  12. Capstone: build a browserMainWeb Browser Engineering — Panchekha & HarrelsonBuild a working browser in Python, chapter by chapter: networking, parsing, styling, layout, JavaScript. It explains why everything in web.dev's performance advice works.

Where value diverges

The Odin Project and Full Stack Open are the two best full-stack paths — Odin is broader and gentler, Full Stack Open a rigorous React, Node and TypeScript deep-dive. Backend Engineering

0 / 5 Essentials · 0 / 52

How production services are built and run: protocols and APIs, identity and security, server concurrency, caching, messaging and workflows, serverless and data pipelines (observability lives in Software Engineering). Do it before System Design: the first seven stages of the Optimal path (fundamentals, API design, building a real API, hard API cases, auth, security, concurrent servers) need nothing from it. Caching and messaging go best once System Design's building blocks are in hand, and data engineering after DDIA. A web full-stack background helps but isn't required.

Optimal path 12 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Backend fundamentalsMainFundamentals of Backend Engineering — Hussein NasserStart here for the vocabulary: request-response, push, pub/sub, HTTP versions, proxies. Watch a section per session and write a two-line summary of each pattern from memory.
  2. Designing APIsMainThe Design of Web APIs (2nd ed.) — Arnaud LauretAlsoRFC 9110: HTTP Semantics — Fielding, Nottingham & ReschkeLauret teaches designing from consumers' needs; sketch each example API before reading his version. Look up methods and status codes in RFC 9110 instead of guessing.
  3. Build a production APIMainLet's Go Further — Alex EdwardsAlsoPostgreSQL Documentation — The PostgreSQL Global Development GroupBuild Edwards's JSON API end to end, typing every line and applying Lauret's design. It assumes basic Go, so learn the syntax first. Read the PostgreSQL docs' MVCC and indexes chapters when databases appear.
  4. Hard API casesMainAPI Design Patterns — JJ GeewaxAlsoAPI Improvement Proposals (AIP) — GooglePracticeImplementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres — Brandur LeachRead Geewax by need: pagination, long-running operations, batch methods. Check the matching AIP rule. Then add idempotency keys to your Let's Go Further API, following Leach.
  5. Identity and authorizationFirstOAuth 2.0 Simplified — Aaron PareckiMainSolving Identity Management in Modern Applications (2nd ed.) — Yvonne Wilson & Abhishek HingnikarAlsoAuthorization Academy — OsoParecki's plain walkthrough of OAuth flows first. Then Wilson & Hingnikar for OAuth 2, OpenID Connect, SAML and sessions end to end. Authorization Academy covers permissions modelling.
  6. Backend securityFirstOWASP Top 10:2025 — OWASPMainWeb Security Academy — PortSwiggerAlsoAPI Security in Action — Neil MaddenSkim the OWASP Top 10 for the map. Then do PortSwigger's lessons and labs: exploit, then fix. Madden's book shows how to build the defences into an API.
  7. Concurrent network serversFirstThe C10K problem — Dan KegelMainProtohackersRead Kegel's survey of server I/O strategies, then implement Protohackers servers to spec. Passing the automated tests is the proof; each problem is a self-contained evening win.
  8. Caching strategiesMainCaching challenges and strategies — Brinkley & Chhabra (Amazon Builders' Library)AlsoScaling Memcache at Facebook — Nishtala et al.PracticeRedis Documentation — RedisRead the Builders' Library article first. Try cache-aside, TTLs and eviction policies hands-on with the Redis docs. Then the Memcache paper for leases against stampedes at scale.
  9. Kafka and event streamingFirstConfluent Developer Courses — ConfluentMainKafka: The Definitive Guide (2nd ed.) — Shapira, Palino, Sivaram & PettyTake Confluent's Kafka 101 for a quick visual start. Then the book for partitions, consumer groups and delivery semantics; Kafka 4 removed ZooKeeper, so skim those parts.
  10. Messaging patterns, consistencyMainmicroservices.io — Chris RichardsonAlsoEnterprise Integration Patterns — Hohpe & WoolfPracticeRabbitMQ Tutorials — RabbitMQRead microservices.io's outbox, saga and idempotent-consumer pages. Do the RabbitMQ tutorials to feel queues hands-on. Dip into Hohpe & Woolf by pattern, not cover to cover.
  11. Elective: durable executionFirstThe Theory of Durable Execution — Jack VanlightlyMainTemporal Courses — TemporalElective. Read Vanlightly's essays for what durable execution guarantees, then build workflows in Temporal's hands-on courses: replay, error handling, sagas, versioning.
  12. Elective: data engineeringMainFundamentals of Data Engineering — Joe Reis & Matt HousleyAlsoStreaming Systems — Akidau, Chernyak & LaxPracticeData Engineering Zoomcamp — DataTalks.ClubElective. Reis & Housley for the lifecycle, building a pipeline in the Zoomcamp alongside. Streaming Systems comes last, after Kafka, for event time, windows and watermarks.
Then, by interest

Course path 12 steps
  1. CourseFundamentals of Backend Engineering — Hussein NasserThe vocabulary: request-response, push, pub/sub, HTTP versions, proxies. Watch a section per session and summarise each pattern from memory.
  2. CourseBoot.devBookPostgreSQL Documentation — The PostgreSQL Global Development GroupBuild HTTP servers with SQL and auth in Boot.dev's back-end path. Read the PostgreSQL docs' MVCC and indexes chapters when databases appear.

  10. CourseRabbitMQ Tutorials — RabbitMQBookmicroservices.io — Chris RichardsonDo the RabbitMQ tutorials to feel queues hands-on. Read microservices.io's outbox, saga and idempotent-consumer pages for consistency.

Textbook path 9 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. The Design of Web APIs (2nd ed.) — Arnaud LauretStart here: design APIs from consumers' needs — resource modelling, OpenAPI contracts, errors, versioning and evolution. Do its exercises before writing any server code.
  2. Let's Go Further — Alex EdwardsBuild the kind of API Lauret taught you to design: a production JSON API in Go with validation, pagination, rate limiting, auth tokens, graceful shutdown. Assumes basic Go.
  3. API Design Patterns — JJ GeewaxThe hard cases after Lauret: pagination, long-running operations, batch methods, request deduplication, filtering. Read the patterns relevant to your work; skim the rest.
  4. Solving Identity Management in Modern Applications (2nd ed.) — Yvonne Wilson & Abhishek HingnikarOAuth 2, OpenID Connect and SAML end to end — tokens, sessions, single sign-on, logout — and which fits each kind of application.
  5. API Security in Action — Neil MaddenSecure an API step by step: cookies, tokens and JWTs, OAuth2, capabilities and service-to-service auth. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy labs pair well.
  6. Kafka: The Definitive Guide (2nd ed.) — Shapira, Palino, Sivaram & PettyPartitions, consumer groups, delivery semantics, idempotent and transactional producers. Kafka 4 removed ZooKeeper, so skim the ZooKeeper operations material.
  7. Enterprise Integration Patterns — Hohpe & WoolfThe broker-agnostic pattern language behind messaging: channels, routers, competing consumers, dead-letter channels, idempotent receivers. Read selectively as a vocabulary after Kafka.
  8. Fundamentals of Data Engineering — Joe Reis & Matt HousleyElective: the data-engineering lifecycle — ingestion, storage, warehouses and lakehouses, batch and streaming, orchestration — as tool-independent principles.
  9. Streaming Systems — Akidau, Chernyak & LaxElective, after Fundamentals of Data Engineering and Kafka: event time, windowing, watermarks, triggers and exactly-once processing in depth.

Where value diverges

Language matters less than it seems: Let's Go Further (Go) and Zero To Production (Rust) teach the same production concerns, so pick the one matching your stack. Vendor-specific resources (Kafka, Temporal, Redis, AWS, Cloudflare) are chosen because they teach the general pattern best; the concepts transfer to their competitors. The last three groups are electives — take them when your work needs them.

System Design & Distributed Systems

Guided path — work in order
0 / 8 Essentials · 0 / 36

How systems behave across many machines: building blocks, scaling, caching, queues, replication, consistency, consensus and failure. Follow the Optimal path: fast building blocks and interview-style practice first, then the deep core (6.1800, DDIA, distributed-systems theory), with the papers as a shelf to browse. Assumes CS networking, databases and operating systems, and goes best after the first stages of Backend Engineering (one service built well before many services at scale); its building blocks then feed Backend's caching and messaging stages; how to structure the code inside each service lives in Software Engineering.

Optimal path 10 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Building blocks fastFirstByteByteGo — Alex Xu & Sahn LamMainHello Interview — System Design in a HurryRead Hello Interview's core concepts and key technologies first; it's a quick, clear win. Watch the matching ByteByteGo animation for anything that feels abstract.
  2. Distributed systems tourMainUnderstanding Distributed Systems — Roberto VitilloAlsoAWS Builder's Library — AmazonRead Vitillo cover to cover, a chapter per session. After the resiliency part, read the Builder's Library articles on timeouts, retries with jitter and load shedding.
  3. Classic designs practiceMainSystem Design Interview, Vol. 1 & 2 — Alex Xu & Sahn LamPracticeawesome-system-design-resources — Ashish Pratap SinghFor each Xu design, sketch your own on paper first, then read. Afterwards pick unsolved problems from awesome-system-design-resources and design them using Vitillo's building blocks.
  4. Why systems look this wayMainMIT 6.1800 (OCW: 6.033) — Computer Systems Engineering — MITAlsoPrinciples of Computer System Design — Jerome Saltzer & M. Frans KaashoekFollow 6.1800's lectures and the papers it assigns: modularity, naming, fault tolerance. Saltzer & Kaashoek is dense; dip into a chapter only when a topic needs depth.
  5. Data-intensive coreFirstThe Log: What Every Software Engineer Should Know About Real-Time Data's Unifying Abstraction — Jay KrepsMainDesigning Data-Intensive Applications (2nd ed.) — Kleppmann & RiccominiThe heart of the path. Read Kreps's essay first for the log as a unifying idea, then DDIA slowly; after each chapter, explain its main trade-off in your own words.
  6. Time, replication, consensusMainDistributed Systems lectures — Martin Kleppmann (Cambridge)AlsoCSE 138 — Distributed Systems — Lindsey Kuper (UC Santa Cruz)PracticeGossip Glomers — Fly.io & Kyle KingsburyKleppmann's compact lectures extend DDIA; do the exercises in his notes. Solve Gossip Glomers alongside. If a topic doesn't land, watch Kuper's slower CSE 138 lecture on it.
  7. Foundational papersMainTime, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System — Leslie LamportAlsoDynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store — DeCandia et al.AlsoSpanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database — Corbett et al.Read Lamport first; it's short. Then Dynamo and Spanner as a pair: availability via quorums and vector clocks versus external consistency via synchronised clocks.
  8. Storage and patternsMainDatabase Internals — Alex PetrovAlsoPatterns of Distributed Systems — Unmesh JoshiPetrov goes below DDIA: B-tree and LSM engines, then failure detection and leader election. Use Joshi's named patterns to connect each idea to Kafka and etcd code.
  9. Build Raft yourselfMainMIT 6.5840 — Distributed Systems — Morris et al. (MIT)AlsoIn Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft) — Diego Ongaro & John OusterhoutThe mastery stage. Read the Raft paper before the Raft lab, then work 6.5840's Go labs: MapReduce, Raft, a sharded store. Expect to debug; that's the learning.
  10. How systems really failMainAphyr — Jepsen analyses — Kyle KingsburyAlsoMarc Brooker's blog — Marc BrookerRead a Jepsen analysis per session and predict the anomaly before he reveals it. Brooker's short essays on retries and metastable failures round out the production view.
Course path 10 steps
  1. CourseHello Interview — System Design in a HurryBookAWS Builder's Library — AmazonRead the core concepts and key technologies; watch the matching ByteByteGo animation as a warm-up when abstract. Then Builder's Library articles on timeouts, retries, load shedding.
  2. CourseJordan Has No Life — System Design 2.0Bookawesome-system-design-resources — Ashish Pratap SinghClassic designs: sketch each problem on paper before watching his deep-dive. Then pick unsolved problems from awesome-system-design-resources and design them yourself.
  3. CourseMIT 6.1800 (OCW: 6.033) — Computer Systems Engineering — MITWhy systems look this way: follow the lectures and the papers they assign on modularity, naming and fault tolerance.
  4. CourseDistributed Systems lectures — Martin Kleppmann (Cambridge)BookThe Log: What Every Software Engineer Should Know About Real-Time Data's Unifying Abstraction — Jay KrepsRead Kreps's essay first. Then Kleppmann's lectures on clocks, replication and consensus, doing his exercises; Kuper's CSE 138 is the slower alternative.
  5. CourseGossip Glomers — Fly.io & Kyle KingsburyBookTime, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System — Leslie LamportSolve the challenges against Jepsen's checker. Read Lamport's short paper alongside the broadcast and counter problems.
  6. BookDynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store — DeCandia et al.Availability via consistent hashing, quorums and vector clocks; list each trade-off against consistency as you read.
  7. BookSpanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database — Corbett et al.Dynamo's counterpoint: external consistency via synchronised clocks. Contrast its choices with Dynamo's in a short table.
  8. CourseMIT 6.5840 — Distributed Systems — Morris et al. (MIT)BookIn Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft) — Diego Ongaro & John OusterhoutThe mastery stage. Read the Raft paper before the Raft lab, then work the Go labs: MapReduce, Raft, a sharded store.
  9. BookAphyr — Jepsen analyses — Kyle KingsburyRead one analysis per session and predict the anomaly before it is revealed.
  10. BookMarc Brooker's blog — Marc BrookerShort essays on retries, backoff and metastable failures that round out the production view.
Textbook path 6 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Understanding Distributed Systems — Roberto VitilloStart here: a compact tour of communication, coordination, scalability, resiliency and operations. Read cover to cover; it gives you the vocabulary for everything after it.
  2. System Design Interview, Vol. 1 & 2 — Alex Xu & Sahn LamApply Vitillo's building blocks to classic designs with a four-step method. Sketch each design yourself before reading its chapter, then compare.
  3. Principles of Computer System Design — Jerome Saltzer & M. Frans KaashoekWhy systems are built this way: modularity, naming, fault tolerance, atomicity, consistency. Dense, so dip into chapters selectively rather than reading straight through; pairs with MIT 6.1800.
  4. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd ed.) — Kleppmann & RiccominiThe core: storage, encoding, replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency, consensus and streams from first principles. Read it all, slowly; Kleppmann's lectures pair well.
  5. Database Internals — Alex PetrovGoes below DDIA: B-tree and LSM storage engines, then failure detection, leader election and consensus as implemented in real databases.
  6. Patterns of Distributed Systems — Unmesh JoshiTurns DDIA's ideas into named implementation patterns (write-ahead log, leader and followers, lease) from Kafka and etcd. Pairs well with building Raft in MIT 6.5840.

Where value diverges

Interview fluency and real mastery are different targets, and this subject serves both. Hello Interview, Vitillo and Xu get most people interview-ready fast; 6.1800, DDIA, Kleppmann's lectures and the 6.5840 labs are what make you genuinely good. AI & Machine Learning

0 / 11 Essentials · 0 / 73

From first models to modern LLMs. Requires the Mathematics essentials (linear algebra, calculus, probability) and comfortable Python. Start with Ng and Géron, go deep with 3Blue1Brown, Karpathy and Prince, then branch into vision, language, RL, engineering and safety.

Optimal path 15 stages

Textbook path 11 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch — Aurélien GéronStart here: the whole ML toolkit in working scikit-learn and PyTorch code. Code along from day one; assumes Python plus basic linear algebra and calculus from the Mathematics path.
  2. An Introduction to Statistical Learning — James et al.Classical methods done properly — regression, resampling, regularization, trees, SVMs, unsupervised learning. Work the Python labs; it explains the why behind Géron's tools.
  3. Neural Networks and Deep Learning — NielsenThe gentlest first deep-learning read: builds a digit classifier and backpropagation from scratch. Short, free online; do the exercises.
  4. Understanding Deep Learning — Simon PrinceThe main deep-learning text — modern and clear, covering transformers, diffusion models and generalization. Run the notebooks for each chapter you read.
  5. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach — Russell & NorvigClassical AI reference — read only the search, constraint-satisfaction, MDP and Bayes-net chapters, not front to back. Pairs well with Berkeley CS188 if you want it.
  6. Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) — Sebastian RaschkaBuild a GPT-style model in plain PyTorch — tokenization, attention, pretraining, instruction fine-tuning. Type every listing; it makes Prince's transformer chapter concrete.
  7. Reinforcement Learning — Sutton & BartoThe foundational RL text, readable with care — bandits, MDPs, TD learning, policy gradients. Part I is the core; go further as interest allows.
  8. Foundations of Computer Vision — Torralba, Isola & FreemanVision elective: unifies signal processing, geometry and learning to explain why vision methods work. Read selectively after Prince.
  9. Designing Machine Learning Systems — Chip HuyenProduction ML around the model: data pipelines, features, deployment, monitoring and drift. Read with a real or imagined system in mind; it sets up AI Engineering.
  10. AI Engineering — Chip HuyenBuilding products on foundation models — prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation and inference cost, organized as an engineering discipline.
  11. Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society — Dan HendrycksCloses the path: an accessible map of AI risk, robustness, alignment, governance and ethics. Read it as a whole; chapters are self-contained.

Where value diverges

Goodfellow was canonical but predates transformers; Prince's Understanding Deep Learning and Bishop's 2024 rewrite are the current texts. Ng's specializations are bottom-up and gentle; fast.ai is the top-down alternative, though its videos date from 2022. For LLMs the classic texts stop short: pair Karpathy's videos with Raschka's build-it books, then CS336 for rigour. Applied LLM engineering (agents, RAG, evals) moves fastest — use Huyen's AI Engineering as the frame and treat the articles as snapshots to re-check yearly.

Game Engines & Graphics

0 / 5 Essentials · 0 / 42

Building renderers, engines and game systems from scratch. Ranked by pedagogy — start structured, then go deep. Requires linear algebra and comfortable C or C++; The Cherno's engine series is the long-form parallel track.

Optimal path 10 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Game math, visuallyMainMath for Game Devs — Freya HolmérAlso3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development — Dunn & ParberryYour gentle start: watch Freya's lectures for the picture, then read the matching 3D Math Primer section and do its exercises to lock it in.
  2. Rendering from first principlesMainComputer Graphics from Scratch — Gabriel GambettaPracticeTinyRenderer — Dmitry SokolovRead Gambetta's short book and code its raytracer and rasterizer yourself. Then write TinyRenderer's software rasterizer to prove you can do it unguided.
  3. Shaders by experimentMainThe Book of Shaders — Patricio Gonzalez VivoA quick, fun win: edit every example live in the browser and try the exercises before moving on. No setup needed.
  4. First GPU rendererMainLearn OpenGL — Joey de VriesAlsoA Trip Through the Graphics Pipeline — Fabian GiesenType every Learn OpenGL chapter yourself, from first triangle onward. Read Giesen's series once your renderer works, to see what the GPU actually does.
  5. Game architecture patternsMainGame Programming Patterns — NystromAlsoGaffer On Games — Glenn FiedlerRead a pattern per evening and sketch where it fits your own code. Read Fiedler's Fix Your Timestep alongside the game-loop chapter.
  6. Build a small engineMainPikuma — Gustavo PezziPick one Pikuma engine course and code along fully; the finished engine becomes the codebase you extend for the rest of this path.
  7. Real engine architectureMainGame Engine Architecture — Jason GregoryAlsoThe Cherno — Hazel / Game Engine SeriesDon't read Gregory cover to cover: read the chapter for whichever subsystem you're building next, and watch the matching Cherno episodes to see it written in C++.
  8. Simulation and procedural motionFirstCoding Adventures — Sebastian LagueMainThe Nature of Code — Daniel ShiffmanCode each Nature of Code example and do its exercises. Watch Coding Adventures for motivation and method, then try a small version yourself.
  9. Game AI and pathfindingFirstRed Blob Games — Amit PatelMainAI for Games — Ian MillingtonPlay with Red Blob Games' interactive A* and grid pages first, then read Millington and implement steering and pathfinding in your engine.
  10. Deeper renderingMainIntroduction to Computer Graphics — Cem Yuksel (Utah)AlsoFundamentals of Computer Graphics — Marschner & ShirleyPracticeRay Tracing in One Weekend — Peter ShirleyWatch Yuksel's lectures in order; build Shirley's weekend ray tracer alongside. Use Marschner & Shirley to look up any topic that didn't land.

Textbook path 7 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. 3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development — Dunn & ParberryStart here: vectors, matrices, transforms, rotations and quaternions explained gently for games. Pairs well with Freya Holmér's videos if you want them.
  2. Computer Graphics from Scratch — Gabriel GambettaBuild a raytracer and a rasterizer with no API in the way, using the 3D math you just learned. Short; code each chapter yourself.
  3. Game Programming Patterns — NystromGame architecture patterns — game loop, update method, components, event queues — clear and funny. Free online; read before your own engine grows.
  4. Game Engine Architecture — Jason GregoryHow real engines are structured, by a Naughty Dog lead. About 1,200 pages: read each chapter as your own engine reaches that subsystem.
  5. The Nature of Code — Daniel ShiffmanSimulation and procedural motion — noise, forces, particles, steering, cellular automata, fractals — built in runnable p5.js sketches. Run and tweak every example.
  6. AI for Games — Ian MillingtonGame AI — steering, pathfinding, decision trees, state machines, behaviour trees, tactical AI. Its steering chapter extends what The Nature of Code introduced.
  7. Fundamentals of Computer Graphics — Marschner & ShirleyDeepen rendering properly: transforms, rasterization, ray tracing, shading and textures as a clear university text, revisiting what Gambetta built with more rigour.

Engineering: Signals, Control & Robotics

0 / 8 Essentials · 0 / 46

How to make physical systems do what you want — the applied layer on top of Physics and Mathematics: mechanics, thermal systems, circuits, measurement, signals, feedback, and machines that act in the world. Requires calculus, linear algebra and differential equations first.

Optimal path 14 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Structures by intuitionFirstThe Efficient EngineerMainStructures: Or Why Things Don't Fall Down — J.E. GordonRead Gordon straight through for pleasure, an evening at a time. When a topic like stress, beams or buckling comes up, watch the matching Efficient Engineer video.
  2. Engineering mechanics and dynamicsMainMIT 2.003SC — Engineering Dynamics — J. Kim Vandiver (MIT)PracticeEngineering Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics — HibbelerWatch a Vandiver lecture and its problem-solving video, then work a few Hibbeler problems on the same topic. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  3. Thermodynamics and heat transferMainThermodynamics and Propulsion — Greitzer, Spakovszky & Waitz (MIT)AlsoA Heat Transfer Textbook — Lienhard IV & Lienhard VPracticeLearnChemE — University of Colorado BoulderRead the MIT notes on the first and second laws and cycles; use LearnChemE screencasts and simulations to practise. Turn to Lienhard for conduction; take convection selectively.
  4. Circuit fundamentalsFirstFalstad Circuit Simulator & applets — Paul FalstadMainPractical Electronics for Inventors — Scherz & MonkRead Scherz & Monk's fundamentals one component at a time, and rebuild each example circuit in Falstad to watch current flow. Skip component chapters until you need them.
  5. Circuits and electronicsMainMIT 6.002 — Circuits and Electronics — Agarwal & Lang (MIT)PracticeLearning the Art of Electronics — Hayes & HorowitzFollow Agarwal's lectures for the abstractions, keep checking circuits in Falstad, and do Hayes & Horowitz labs at a real breadboard. Building beats reading here.
  6. Measurement and uncertaintyMainAn Introduction to Error Analysis — John R. TaylorShort and very clear: read a chapter per session and work the end-of-chapter problems. Apply error propagation to your own breadboard measurements.
  7. How things are madeFirstManufacturing Processes for Design Professionals — Rob ThompsonMainFundamentals of Manufacturing Processes (2.008x) — A. John Hart et al. (MITx)Take the 2.008x course for rate, quality, cost and flexibility trade-offs; flip through Thompson's visual step-by-step pages to see each process. A lighter stage; pace it as a breather.
  8. Signals made concreteMainThe Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing — Steven W. SmithPracticeThink DSP — Allen B. DowneyRead Smith's foundational chapters on sampling, convolution, Fourier and filters; skim the applications. Code the same ideas in Think DSP's Python exercises.
  9. Signals and systems formallyMainMIT 6.003 — Signals and Systems — Dennis Freeman (MIT)PracticeSignals and Systems — Oppenheim & WillskyWatch Freeman's lectures and do the problem sets; use Oppenheim & Willsky for extra worked examples and problems. Prioritise Laplace and z-transforms, which control builds on.
  10. Classical feedback controlFirstControl System Lectures — Brian DouglasMainControl Systems Engineering — Norman NiseWatch Brian Douglas's video on a topic first, then work Nise's step-by-step examples and case studies: modelling, transient response, stability, root locus, frequency response.
  11. State-space controlMainControl Bootcamp — Steve Brunton (UW)AlsoFeedback Systems — Åström & MurrayOnce Nise feels routine, watch Brunton for controllability, LQR and observers, running his code. Read Åström & Murray's state-feedback and observer chapters as the written second voice.
  12. State estimationMainKalman and Bayesian Filters in Python — Roger LabbeRun and modify Labbe's notebooks from g-h filters up through Kalman, extended and unscented filters. Assumes basic probability from the Mathematics path.
  13. Robot mechanicsMainModern Robotics — Lynch & Park (Northwestern)PracticeRobotics, Vision and Control — Peter CorkeWork Modern Robotics' short videos and exercises on kinematics, dynamics, planning and control; run Corke's Python on arms and mobile robots to make each idea tangible.
  14. Robots under uncertaintyMainProbabilistic Robotics — Thrun, Burgard & FoxDenser than earlier books: focus on localization and mapping, applying the Kalman and particle filters from Labbe to whole robots. Read slowly, a section per session.
Then, by interest
  • Digital Design & Hardware — start with Digital Design and Computer Architecture — David Harris & Sarah Harris
  • Aerospace & Flight — start with Introduction to Flight — John D. Anderson Jr. & Mary L. Bowden
Course path 9 steps
  1. CourseThe Efficient EngineerBookTo Engineer Is Human — Henry PetroskiStructures by intuition: watch the videos on stress, beams and buckling, and read Petroski on what each structural failure teaches designers.
  2. CourseMIT 2.003SC — Engineering Dynamics — J. Kim Vandiver (MIT)Kinematics, rigid bodies, work-energy and vibration. Watch a lecture and its problem-solving video, then do the problem set. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  3. CourseThermodynamics and Propulsion — Greitzer, Spakovszky & Waitz (MIT)Read the notes on the first and second laws, entropy and cycles, then heat transfer. LearnChemE — University of Colorado Boulder screencasts are the alternative for practice.
  4. CourseMIT 6.002 — Circuits and Electronics — Agarwal & Lang (MIT)Circuits as layers of abstraction, lumped elements to amplifiers. Warm up by rebuilding each circuit in the Falstad Circuit Simulator to watch current flow.
  5. CourseFundamentals of Manufacturing Processes (2.008x) — A. John Hart et al. (MITx)BookManufacturing Processes for Design Professionals — Rob ThompsonHow things are made, judged by rate, quality, cost and flexibility. Flip through Thompson’s step-by-step pages for each process. A lighter breather stage.
  6. CourseMIT 6.003 — Signals and Systems — Dennis Freeman (MIT)Convolution, Fourier, Laplace and z-transforms: the shared language of control and DSP. Do the problem sets, prioritising Laplace and z-transforms.
  7. CourseControl System Lectures — Brian DouglasClassical feedback: transfer functions, stability, root locus and Bode plots made visual. Sketch each plot by hand before he reveals it.
  8. CourseControl Bootcamp — Steve Brunton (UW)State-space control: controllability, LQR, observers and the Kalman filter. Run and modify his code for each lecture.
  9. CourseModern Robotics — Lynch & Park (Northwestern)Robot mechanics: kinematics, dynamics, planning and control from one screw-theory foundation. Watch the short videos, then do the exercises and code.
Textbook path 13 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Structures: Or Why Things Don't Fall Down — J.E. GordonStart here for intuition: stress, strain, stiffness and why structures stand or fail, told with almost no equations. Read it straight through for pleasure.
  2. Engineering Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics — HibbelerYour working mechanics text: forces, equilibrium, then particle and rigid-body dynamics through many worked examples. Do a few problems per section; assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  3. A Heat Transfer Textbook — Lienhard IV & Lienhard VFree online: conduction, convection, radiation and heat exchangers, built from energy balances. Read the introductory chapters and conduction carefully; take convection and boiling more selectively.
  4. Practical Electronics for Inventors — Scherz & MonkThe gentle on-ramp to circuits: voltage, current, components and basic circuits explained one part at a time. Read the fundamentals first; dip into component chapters as needed.
  5. Learning the Art of Electronics — Hayes & HorowitzNow build: Hayes & Horowitz's lab-based book, from passive circuits through transistors, op-amps and digital logic to microcontrollers. Do the labs at a breadboard rather than just reading.
  6. An Introduction to Error Analysis — John R. TaylorHow to judge any measurement: uncertainty, error propagation, repeated-measurement statistics and least-squares fitting. Short and very clear; work the end-of-chapter problems.
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing — Steven W. SmithFree online and plain-spoken: sampling, convolution, the Fourier transform and filters explained before the maths. Read the foundational chapters; skim the application chapters.
  8. Signals and Systems — Oppenheim & WillskyThe full signals-and-systems treatment: continuous and discrete time, Fourier, Laplace and z-transforms. Slower going than Smith; work the examples, since control builds on Laplace.
  9. Control Systems Engineering — Norman NiseYour main control text: modelling, transient response, stability, root locus, frequency response and design, all through step-by-step worked examples. Work the examples and case studies.
  10. Feedback Systems — Åström & MurrayFree second control book: the same feedback ideas seen conceptually, then state-space models, state feedback and observers. Read once Nise's methods feel routine.
  11. Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python — Roger LabbeFree Jupyter book: state estimation from intuition up — g-h, Kalman, extended and unscented filters. Run and modify the notebooks; assumes basic probability from the Mathematics path.
  12. Robotics, Vision and Control — Peter CorkeRobot mechanics with runnable Python: poses, arm kinematics and dynamics, mobile robots and vision-based control. Read the arm and mobile-robot parts, running the code as you go.
  13. Probabilistic Robotics — Thrun, Burgard & FoxLocalization, mapping and SLAM under uncertainty, applying the Kalman and particle filters from Labbe to whole robots. Denser than earlier books; focus on the localization and mapping chapters.

Where value diverges

Brian Douglas builds the intuition; Åström & Murray supplies the rigour — use both, in that order. Oppenheim & Willsky is the canonical signals text but a hard first read; Smith's DSP guide reaches working intuition faster. Modern Robotics subsumes most older robotics texts; Probabilistic Robotics complements it with uncertainty rather than mechanics. Several classic MIT mechanics and fluids courses are problem sets without video, so pair them with The Efficient Engineer and the fluid mechanics films.

Economics, Finance & Decision

0 / 10 Essentials · 0 / 48

How markets, policy, judgment and cause-and-effect actually work: intro economics, decision-making, micro and game theory, causal inference, macro and finance. Basic algebra and introductory statistics help from micro onward.

Optimal path 9 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Economics from real dataFirstMarginal Revolution University — Cowen & TabarrokMainThe Economy 2.0 — The CORE TeamRead CORE's microeconomics volume first, a unit per week; when a concept won't click, watch the matching short Marginal Revolution University video for a second explanation.
  2. Judgment and decisionsFirstThinking, Fast and Slow — KahnemanMainRational Choice in an Uncertain World — Reid Hastie & Robyn DawesRead Hastie & Dawes cover to cover; it needs only basic probability. Dip into Kahneman for vivid examples of heuristics and prospect theory, skipping the priming chapter.
  3. Intermediate microeconomicsMainIntermediate Microeconomics — VarianAlsoMIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics — Jonathan Gruber (MIT)PracticeWorkouts in Intermediate Microeconomics — Bergstrom & VarianRead a Varian chapter, then solve its Workouts problems; micro is learned by solving. Watch the matching Gruber lecture only when a chapter feels abstract. Assumes basic calculus from the Mathematics path.
  4. Game theoryFirstThe Art of Strategy — Dixit & NalebuffMainGame Theory (ECON 159) — Ben Polak (Open Yale)PracticeGames of Strategy — Dixit, Skeath & McAdamsRead The Art of Strategy's stories for intuition, follow Polak's lectures as the spine, and compute equilibria with Games of Strategy exercises on each topic.
  5. Causal inference basicsFirstMastering Econometrics — Joshua Angrist (Marginal Revolution University)MainMastering 'Metrics — Angrist & PischkeWatch Angrist's short video on each tool, then read the matching chapter of Mastering 'Metrics: experiments, regression, instruments, regression discontinuity, differences-in-differences. Short; read it all.
  6. Research design with codeMainThe Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality — Nick Huntington-KleinAlsoThe Effect Video Series — Nick Huntington-KleinRead The Effect's causal-diagram chapters, watching the author's short video for each, and run the code examples. It deepens Mastering 'Metrics rather than repeating it.
  7. Intermediate macroeconomicsMainMacroeconomics — BlanchardAlsoMIT 14.02 Principles of Macroeconomics — Ricardo Caballero (MIT)PracticeChair the Fed & The Fiscal ShipRead CORE's macroeconomics volume first, then Blanchard, watching Caballero's lecture on the same topic. After monetary and fiscal policy, play Chair the Fed and The Fiscal Ship.
  8. Financial marketsMainFinancial Markets — Robert Shiller (Yale)AlsoA Random Walk Down Wall Street — Burton MalkielFollow Shiller's lectures on risk, efficiency and behavioural finance; read Malkiel's readable tour alongside for what it means for your own investing.

Corporate finance and valuationMainCorporate Finance & Valuation — Aswath Damodaran (NYU)PracticePrinciples of Corporate Finance — Brealey, Myers, Allen & EdmansWatch Damodaran's classes and value a real company yourself; work Brealey & Myers' worked examples on present value, capital budgeting and cost of capital.

Course path 10 steps
  1. CourseMarginal Revolution University — Cowen & TabarrokBookThe Worldly Philosophers — Robert HeilbronerWork MRU's principles videos in order: supply and demand, markets, trade, institutions. Read Heilbroner alongside for where each idea came from.

  6. CourseThe Effect Video Series — Nick Huntington-KleinBookThe Book of Why — Pearl & MackenzieCausal diagrams and research design. Read Pearl for the intuition behind diagrams, then draw one for a causal question at work.
  7. CourseMIT 14.02 Principles of Macroeconomics — Ricardo Caballero (MIT)Intro macro: output, money, inflation, unemployment, open economies and crises.
  8. CourseChair the Fed & The Fiscal ShipBookLords of Finance — Liaquat AhamedSet interest rates and balance a budget to feel the trade-offs from Caballero's lectures; Ahamed shows real central bankers getting it wrong before the Depression.
  9. CourseFinancial Markets — Robert Shiller (Yale)BookA Random Walk Down Wall Street — Burton MalkielRisk, efficiency and behavioural finance from Shiller; Malkiel's readable tour shows what it means for your own investing.
  10. CourseCorporate Finance & Valuation — Aswath Damodaran (NYU)Investment decisions, cost of capital and discounted cash flow. Value one real company yourself in a spreadsheet as you go.
Textbook path 8 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. The Economy 2.0 — The CORE TeamStart here: free, data-driven principles in microeconomics and macroeconomics volumes. Read the microeconomics volume first; the macroeconomics volume prepares you for Blanchard later on this path.
  2. Rational Choice in an Uncertain World — Reid Hastie & Robyn DawesThe decision-making thread: probability judgment, expected utility, heuristics and biases, and how to decide better. Readable cover to cover; needs only basic probability.
  3. Intermediate Microeconomics — VarianMicro done properly: choice, demand, production, markets, welfare and information, with light calculus. Work the chapter problems; assumes basic calculus from the Mathematics path.
  4. Games of Strategy — Dixit, Skeath & McAdamsStrategic reasoning: sequential and simultaneous games, equilibria, repeated games and applications, taught through examples. Builds on Varian's game-theory chapters; work the exercises.
  5. Mastering 'Metrics — Angrist & PischkeCausal inference made friendly: experiments, regression, instruments, regression discontinuity and differences-in-differences, each told through real studies. Short; read it all.
  6. The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality — Nick Huntington-KleinFree online: causal diagrams and identification from scratch, then the standard methods with code. Deepens Mastering 'Metrics; run the code examples.
  7. Macroeconomics — BlanchardIntermediate macro: goods, money and labour markets, short, medium and long run, growth and policy, anchored in real episodes. Builds on CORE's macroeconomics volume.
  8. Principles of Corporate Finance — Brealey, Myers, Allen & EdmansFinance and valuation: present value, capital budgeting, risk and return, market efficiency, financing and payout. Covers both financial markets and corporate decisions; work the examples.

Where value diverges

CORE's The Economy 2.0 is the consensus neutral, evidence-first start; Mankiw is the traditional alternative. For causal inference, Mastering 'Metrics, the Mixtape and The Effect have largely superseded Mostly Harmless for self-learners. Mind & Society

0 / 5 Essentials · 0 / 33

How minds, languages, societies and institutions work: psychology, linguistics, sociology, political science and law. Read with an eye on evidence — Science Fictions, early on, shows which famous findings held up.

Optimal path 10 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. The map of psychologyMainIntroduction to Psychology (Yale) — Paul BloomPracticeOpenStax Psychology — OpenStaxWatch one Bloom lecture per session, then read the matching OpenStax section and answer its review questions to fix what you heard.
  2. Social psychologyMainSocial Psychology — Gilovich, Keltner, Chen & NisbettRead a chapter per week: attribution, conformity, persuasion, prejudice and groups. For each experiment, predict the result before reading it, then note where your intuition failed.
  3. Thinking like a sociologistFirstThe Sociological Imagination — MillsMainYou May Ask Yourself: An Introduction to Thinking Like a Sociologist — Dalton ConleyRead Mills's opening essay first for the habit of seeing private troubles as public issues, then Conley cover to cover; it is the most engaging entry.
  4. Founders of social theoryMainFoundations of Modern Social Theory (SOCY 151) — Iván Szelényi (Yale)AlsoThe Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism — WeberFollow Szelényi's lectures from Hobbes through Marx, Weber and Durkheim; read Weber's Protestant Ethic alongside his Weber lectures as a model of sociological method.
  5. Political philosophyMainAn Introduction to Political Philosophy — Jonathan WolffAlsoThe Moral Foundations of Politics — Ian Shapiro (Yale)Read Wolff whole: it is short and patient. Watch Shapiro's lectures selectively for the Enlightenment traditions (utilitarianism, Marxism, social contract) Wolff touches on.
  6. Democratic institutionsMainPatterns of Democracy — LijphartRead the framework chapters on majoritarian versus consensus democracy first; skim the country detail. Classify your own country's institutions as you go.
  7. Collective action in practiceMainGoverning the Commons — Elinor OstromRead Ostrom's field cases of communities governing shared resources; list her design principles and test them against a shared resource in your work or town.
  8. How law worksMainLaw 101 — Jay M. FeinmanAlsoContract Law: From Trust to Promise to Contract — Charles Fried (HarvardX)Read Law 101 for the plain-language map, closely on contracts; take Fried's course alongside the contract chapters to reason through real cases.
  9. Legal reasoningMainThinking Like a Lawyer — Frederick SchauerRead after Law 101, once you have doctrine to reason about: rules, precedent, analogy and interpretation. Apply each chapter to a case from Fried's course.
  10. Linguistics (elective)FirstCrash Course Linguistics — Taylor BehnkeMainLanguage Files — Department of Linguistics, The Ohio State UniversityElective: watch the matching Crash Course episode first, then read the Language Files chapter and work its exercises. Dip into the chapters that interest you.
Course path 8 steps
  1. CourseIntroduction to Psychology (Yale) — Paul BloomOne lecture per session: brain, development, perception, memory, social and clinical psychology. Write a three-line summary after each.
  2. BookThe Sociological Imagination — MillsThe habit of seeing private troubles as public issues. Read the opening essay closely and apply it to one workplace problem.
  3. CourseFoundations of Modern Social Theory (SOCY 151) — Iván Szelényi (Yale)BookThe Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism — WeberFollow the lectures from Hobbes through Marx, Weber and Durkheim; read Weber alongside his Weber lectures as a model of sociological method.
  4. CourseThe Moral Foundations of Politics — Ian Shapiro (Yale)The ideas used to justify political authority: utilitarianism, Marxism, social contract and democracy. Note which arguments you find strongest, and why.
  5. BookGoverning the Commons — Elinor OstromField cases of communities governing shared resources. List her design principles and test them against a shared resource in your work or town.
  6. CourseContract Law: From Trust to Promise to Contract — Charles Fried (HarvardX)Legal reasoning through real contract cases: offer, consideration, breach. Brief each case yourself before hearing Fried's analysis.
  7. BookThe Rule of Law — BinghamA senior judge on what the rule of law requires in practice, written for non-lawyers. Read after Fried to widen from contracts to the whole system.
  8. CourseCrash Course Linguistics — Taylor BehnkeBookThrough the Language Glass — Guy DeutscherElective: how language works, from sounds to meaning. Then Deutscher sorts what the evidence says about language shaping perception.
Textbook path 9 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Psychology — Schacter et al.Start here: the broad map of psychology — methods, brain, perception, memory, development, social and clinical — clearly written. Read a chapter per week; use its review questions.
  2. Social Psychology — Gilovich, Keltner, Chen & NisbettDeeper social psychology: attribution, conformity, persuasion, prejudice and groups, grounded in experiments. Read after Schacter's social psychology chapter.
  3. You May Ask Yourself: An Introduction to Thinking Like a Sociologist — Dalton ConleySociology as a way of thinking: class, race, gender, family and institutions through stories and real research. The most engaging entry; read it cover to cover.
  4. Sociology — Giddens & SuttonA big survey to use selectively: read the chapters on sociological theory and research methods to meet the founders, then any topic Conley leaves you curious about.
  5. An Introduction to Political Philosophy — Jonathan WolffWhy political authority is justified: the state, democracy, liberty, property and justice, argued patiently. Short; read it whole.
  6. Patterns of Democracy — LijphartFrom theory to institutions: compares majoritarian and consensus democracies and how their designs perform. Read the framework chapters first; skim the country detail.
  7. Law 101 — Jay M. FeinmanHow the legal system works: US constitutional, contract, tort, property and criminal law in plain language. Read the contract chapters closely.
  8. Thinking Like a Lawyer — Frederick SchauerWhat makes legal reasoning distinctive: rules, precedent, analogy, authority and interpretation. Read after Law 101, once you have doctrine to reason about.
  9. Language Files — Department of Linguistics, The Ohio State UniversityElective: how language is structured — phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and sociolinguistics. Work the exercises; dip into chapters that interest you.

Where value diverges

Psychology findings vary in robustness: trust effects replicated in large preregistered studies, and treat single famous experiments (social priming, ego depletion, power posing) with caution. Politics and law split between normative questions (what should be: Shapiro, Hart) and empirical ones (what is: Lijphart, Ostrom, Blattman); do both. Behavioral economics lives in Economics & Decision; Thinking, Fast and Slow there is the taught version of the papers here.

Philosophy

0 / 14 Essentials · 0 / 82

Two ways in, used together: branch textbooks teach how philosophers argue about a problem, and primary sources, read with Kenny's history beside them, show where the arguments came from. Start with the survey and logic.

Optimal path 13 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. The map of philosophyMainA Little History of Philosophy — Nigel WarburtonAlsoGreat Minds of the Western Intellectual Tradition — Michael SugrueRead one short Warburton chapter per session. When a thinker grabs you, watch Sugrue's lecture on them for context; skip the rest of Sugrue freely.
  2. Doing philosophy yourselfFirstWhat Does It All Mean? — Thomas NagelMainThink — BlackburnRead Nagel's 100 plain pages first as a warm-up, then Blackburn straight through. After each chapter, write a paragraph arguing the side you disagree with.
  3. Formal logicMainIntroduction to Logic — Michael Genesereth (Stanford)Practiceforall x: Calgary — P.D. Magnus, Tim Button, Aaron Thomas-Bolduc & Richard ZachWork Genesereth's interactive exercises, which give immediate feedback, then consolidate with forall x's natural-deduction exercises; that practice is where it sticks.
  4. Moral theoriesFirstJustice — Michael Sandel (Harvard)MainThe Fundamentals of Ethics — Russ Shafer-LandauWatch Sandel's lecture on a theory to feel the dilemma, then read Shafer-Landau's chapter on it, one per sitting, testing each argument and objection.
  5. Political philosophyMainAn Introduction to Political Philosophy — Jonathan WolffAlsoOn Liberty / Utilitarianism — J.S. MillRead Wolff whole: the state, democracy, liberty, property, justice. Then read Mill's short originals as the source behind Wolff's liberty chapter and Shafer-Landau's consequentialism.
  6. Plato and SocratesMainRepublic (and earlier dialogues) — PlatoAlsoIntroduction to Political Philosophy — Steven B. Smith (Yale)Read Euthyphro, Apology and Crito first, then the Republic, a book at a time, with Smith's Yale lectures guiding each part.
  7. Aristotle's ethicsMainNicomachean Ethics — AristotleAlsoA History of Philosophy — Arthur Holmes (Wheaton)Read Irwin's annotated translation of the Nicomachean Ethics alongside Holmes's Aristotle lectures; compare his virtue ethics with Shafer-Landau's chapter on it.
  8. Descartes and doubtFirstThe Great Philosophers — Bryan Magee (BBC)MainMeditations — DescartesAlsoEarly Modern Texts — Jonathan BennettWatch Magee's Descartes episode with Bernard Williams, then read the short Meditations; use Bennett's lightly modernised version when the prose resists.
  9. Hume and inductionMainAn Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding — HumeAlsoThe Problems of Philosophy — Bertrand RussellRead Hume's Enquiry on causation, induction and scepticism (Bennett's version helps), then Russell's short classic, which restates the problem of induction in plain modern prose.
  10. Knowledge and justificationMainWhat Is This Thing Called Knowledge? — Duncan PritchardAlsoGeneral Philosophy — Peter Millican (Oxford)Read Pritchard's short chapters and answer the study questions at each end. Watch Millican's Oxford lectures on scepticism, knowledge and personal identity as a second voice.
  11. Metaphysics puzzlesMainRiddles of Existence — Conee & SiderTake one puzzle per session: personal identity, fatalism, time, God, free will, universals. Pairs with Blackburn's free-will chapter; argue each puzzle both ways in writing.
  12. Mind and bodyMainPhilosophy of Mind — Jaegwon KimAlsoPhilosophy of Mind — John Searle (Berkeley)Kim is more demanding: read slowly, a section at a time, through behaviourism, identity theory and functionalism. Watch Searle's lectures for a vivid, opinionated counter-voice, including the Chinese Room.
  13. Philosophy of scienceMainTheory and Reality — Peter Godfrey-SmithRead last: positivism, Popper, Kuhn, Lakatos, Feyerabend, Bayesianism and realism. It uses the logic from forall x lightly; summarise each school in three sentences.
Then, by interest
  • Applied Ethics & Technology — start with Practical Ethics — Peter Singer
  • Non-Western Philosophy — start with Introduction to Classical Chinese Philosophy — Bryan Van Norden

Course path 14 steps
  1. CourseGreat Minds of the Western Intellectual Tradition — Michael SugrueBookA Little History of Philosophy — Nigel WarburtonRead one short Warburton chapter per session. When a thinker grabs you, watch Sugrue's lecture on them; skip the rest freely.
  2. BookWhat Does It All Mean? — Thomas NagelPhilosophy as doing: nine big questions in about 100 plain pages. After each chapter, write a paragraph arguing the side you disagree with.
  3. CourseIntroduction to Logic — Michael Genesereth (Stanford)Propositional and relational logic. Do every interactive exercise; the immediate feedback is where it sticks.
  4. CourseJustice — Michael Sandel (Harvard)One lecture per evening: utilitarianism, libertarianism, Kant, Rawls, Aristotle. Pause at each dilemma and write your own answer before the class argues it.
  5. BookOn Liberty / Utilitarianism — J.S. MillRead Mill's short originals: the harm principle and the higher pleasures, the sources behind Sandel's lectures on Bentham and Mill.
  6. CourseIntroduction to Political Philosophy — Steven B. Smith (Yale)BookRepublic (and earlier dialogues) — PlatoRead Euthyphro, Apology and Crito first, then the Republic a book at a time, with Smith's Plato lectures guiding each part.
  7. CourseA History of Philosophy — Arthur Holmes (Wheaton)BookNicomachean Ethics — AristotleWatch Holmes's Aristotle lectures beside the Nicomachean Ethics; compare its virtue ethics with Sandel's Aristotle lectures.
  8. CourseThe Great Philosophers — Bryan Magee (BBC)BookMeditations — DescartesWatch Magee's Descartes episode with Bernard Williams, then read the short Meditations. If the prose resists, use Early Modern Texts — Jonathan Bennett.
  9. BookAn Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding — HumeEmpiricism, causation, induction and scepticism. Read a section per session; Bennett's Early Modern Texts version helps with hard passages.
  10. CourseGeneral Philosophy — Peter Millican (Oxford)BookThe Problems of Philosophy — Bertrand RussellMillican's Oxford lectures on scepticism, knowledge, induction, personal identity and free will; Russell's short classic restates these problems in plain prose.
  11. CourseDeath (PHIL 176) — Shelly Kagan (Yale)Metaphysics by doing it: the soul, personal identity and whether death is bad. Note each argument Kagan builds and where you would push back.
  12. CoursePhilosophy of Mind — John Searle (Berkeley)Dualism, behaviourism, functionalism, consciousness and the Chinese Room, from its author: a vivid, opinionated tour of the mind-body debate.
  13. BookThe Logic of Scientific Discovery — PopperPhilosophy of science: read the opening chapters on falsifiability and the demarcation of science. Summarise Popper's view in three sentences.
  14. BookThe Structure of Scientific Revolutions — KuhnParadigms, normal science and revolutions. Read it against Popper: where does Kuhn think falsification fails as a description of real science?
Textbook path 8 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Think — BlackburnStart here: a lively, problem-by-problem introduction to knowledge, mind, free will, God and ethics that teaches you to argue. Read straight through.
  2. forall x: Calgary — P.D. Magnus, Tim Button, Aaron Thomas-Bolduc & Richard ZachFree logic text: truth tables, natural deduction and first-order logic. Do the exercises in each chapter; the natural-deduction practice is where it sticks.
  3. The Fundamentals of Ethics — Russ Shafer-LandauEthics: theories of the good life, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue, contractarianism and metaethics, argument by argument. Read a chapter per sitting and test each argument.
  4. An Introduction to Political Philosophy — Jonathan WolffPolitical philosophy: why have a state, democracy, liberty, property and justice. Short and lucid; read it before the classic primary sources.
  5. What Is This Thing Called Knowledge? — Duncan PritchardEpistemology in short chapters: knowledge, justification, perception, testimony and scepticism, with study questions. Answer the questions at chapter ends.
  6. Riddles of Existence — Conee & SiderMetaphysics made accessible: personal identity, fatalism, time, God, free will and universals, each as a puzzle. Pairs with the free-will discussion in Blackburn.
  7. Philosophy of Mind — Jaegwon KimThe mind-body problem mapped: behaviourism, identity theory, functionalism, mental causation and consciousness. More demanding than earlier books; read slowly, a section at a time.
  8. Theory and Reality — Peter Godfrey-SmithPhilosophy of science: logical positivism, Popper, Kuhn, Lakatos, Feyerabend, Bayesianism and realism. Uses the logic from forall x lightly; read last.

Where value diverges

Read a survey (Kenny) in parallel with the primary sources, not instead of them. The branch textbooks are the fastest way to learn to think in a subfield. History, Strategy & Power

0 / 9 Essentials · 0 / 78

The long arc of civilization, the logic of power, and the lives that show judgment in action. Start with the one-volume world history, then work through the eras, the wider world, economic history and strategy; read the lives as case studies in decision-making.

Optimal path 14 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. The big pictureFirstCrash Course World History — John GreenMainThe Penguin History of the World — Roberts & WestadWatch Crash Course for a quick visual map of the whole sweep. Then read Penguin History steadily; it is long, so let it run in the background alongside the next stages.
  2. First civilisationsFirstFall of Civilizations — Paul CooperMainA History of the Ancient Near East — Marc Van De MieroopRead Van De Mieroop on Mesopotamia, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon and Persia; Egypt appears only through its contacts with them. Use relevant Fall of Civilizations episodes as vivid evening listening.
  3. Ancient GreeceMainIntroduction to Ancient Greek History — Donald Kagan (Yale)AlsoThe Histories — HerodotusFollow Kagan's lectures in order. Read the matching parts of Herodotus during the early lectures, ideally in the Landmark edition with its maps.
  4. Thucydides on powerMainHistory of the Peloponnesian War — ThucydidesRead during or right after Kagan's later lectures, in the Landmark edition. Focus on the speeches and the Melian Dialogue: fear, honour and interest between states.
  5. Ancient RomeFirstThe History of Rome — Mike DuncanMainSPQR — Mary BeardAlsoLives — PlutarchRead SPQR as the core. Read paired Greek and Roman lives in Plutarch as case studies in judgment; play Duncan's podcast on commutes if you want more narrative.
  6. Medieval EuropeMainThe Early Middle Ages — Paul Freedman (Yale)AlsoMedieval Europe — Chris WickhamWatch Freedman's lectures for Rome's transformation up to 1000, then read Wickham to carry the story to 1500.
  7. Science before 1450MainThe Beginnings of Western Science — David C. LindbergRead Lindberg for how ancient, Islamic and medieval thinkers understood nature; it connects the Greek and medieval stages you have just covered.
  8. Beyond EuropeMainThe Silk Roads — Peter FrankopanRe-centre world history on the lands linking China, Persia and the Mediterranean. Afterwards, add one regional history, of China, India or the Arab world, if a region grabs you.
  9. Revolutions and modern EuropeMainEuropean Civilization, 1648–1945 — John Merriman (Yale)AlsoA History of Modern Europe — John MerrimanWatch Merriman's lectures in order; read the matching chapters of his textbook, in the same voice, for anything a lecture rushes past.
  10. Why nations grew richMainGlobal Economic History: A Very Short Introduction — Robert C. AllenAbout 150 pages weighing the rival explanations for growth. Read it before any single-thesis book, and note which explanation you find strongest.
  11. Europe 1914–1949MainTo Hell and Back: Europe 1914–1949 — Ian KershawEurope's age of catastrophe as clear narrative: two world wars and what drove them. Read a chapter per session.
  12. Europe since 1945MainPostwar — Tony JudtReconstruction, Cold War division, integration and 1989 in depth. Long but readable; one section per evening.
  13. Strategic thoughtMainStrategy: A History — Lawrence FreedmanHow strategic thinking evolved from antiquity to business and revolution. Connect each chapter back to Thucydides and the wars you have read about.
  14. Judgment from historyMainThinking in Time — Richard Neustadt & Ernest MayThe capstone for a manager: how decision-makers use and misuse historical analogies. Apply its methods to a real decision you face at work.
Then, by interest
  • Historiography & Method — start with The Landscape of History — John Lewis Gaddis
  • American History — start with The American Yawp — Joseph Locke & Ben Wright (eds.)
Course path 13 steps
  1. CourseCrash Course World History — John GreenBookThe Penguin History of the World — Roberts & WestadWatch Crash Course for a quick visual map of the whole sweep, then read Penguin History steadily in the background alongside the next stages.
  2. CourseFall of Civilizations — Paul CooperThe first civilisations through their collapse, told from their own sources. Pick the episodes on Sumer and the Bronze Age collapse as evening listening.
  3. CourseIntroduction to Ancient Greek History — Donald Kagan (Yale)BookThe Histories — HerodotusFollow Kagan's lectures in order; read the matching parts of Herodotus during the early lectures, ideally the Landmark edition with its maps.
  4. BookHistory of the Peloponnesian War — ThucydidesRead during or after Kagan's later lectures. Focus on the speeches and the Melian Dialogue: fear, honour and interest between states.
  5. BookSPQR — Mary BeardRome from its legends to 212 CE, and how historians argue from scant evidence. The History of Rome — Mike Duncan is an optional commute companion.
  6. BookLives — PlutarchPaired Greek and Roman statesmen as case studies in judgment. Read one pair per session and note the decision that made or broke each man.
  7. CourseThe Early Middle Ages — Paul Freedman (Yale)BookMedieval Europe — Chris WickhamFreedman's lectures carry Rome's transformation to about 1000; then read Wickham to take the story on to 1500.
  8. BookThe Silk Roads — Peter FrankopanRe-centre world history on the lands linking China, Persia and the Mediterranean. Vivid but sweeping; note where it challenges a Europe-first story.
  9. CourseEuropean Civilization, 1648–1945 — John Merriman (Yale)Watch Merriman's lectures in order: absolutism, the French Revolution, industrialisation, empire and the world wars.
  10. BookGlobal Economic History: A Very Short Introduction — Robert C. AllenAbout 150 pages weighing the rival explanations for why some countries grew rich. Note which explanation you find strongest.
  11. BookTo Hell and Back: Europe 1914–1949 — Ian KershawEurope's age of catastrophe as clear narrative: two world wars and what drove them. One chapter per session.
  12. BookPostwar — Tony JudtReconstruction, Cold War division, integration and 1989 in depth. Long but readable; one section per evening.
  13. BookStrategy: A History — Lawrence FreedmanHow strategic thought evolved from antiquity to business and revolution. Connect each chapter back to Thucydides and the wars you have read about.
Textbook path 4 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. A History of the Ancient Near East — Marc Van De MieroopBegin with the first civilisations: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Hittites and Persia, c. 3000–323 BC. A concise standard text; read it straight through with the maps.
  2. The Beginnings of Western Science — David C. LindbergAncient and medieval thought through science, from Mesopotamia and Greece via Islam to medieval universities, to 1450 — the intellectual thread beside Van De Mieroop's political story.
  3. A History of Modern Europe — John MerrimanEurope from the Renaissance to the present: revolutions, industry, empire, two world wars and after, in a lively storyteller's voice. Pairs well with his Yale lectures if wanted.
  4. Thinking in Time — Richard Neustadt & Ernest MayThe strategy-and-judgment capstone: how decision-makers use and misuse historical analogies, with case studies. Apply its method to the history you read in Merriman.

Where value diverges

Several books here argue a thesis rather than report consensus: Why Nations Fail (institutions), Hobsbawm (from the left), Kennedy (imperial overstretch), Frankopan (an Asia-centred sweep). Read them as arguments to test, and use Allen's short economic history to see the rival explanations side by side. Older classics such as Tuchman and the Durants stay for their craft and reflection, not as the current scholarly view.

Literature

0 / 10 Essentials · 0 / 86

Civilizational literacy — primary texts, not summaries. After How to Read, the groups run roughly chronologically, then out to the wider world; each opens with a start-here, and translations are named where the choice matters.

Optimal path 15 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. How to read fictionMainHow to Read Literature Like a Professor — FosterAlsoThe American Novel Since 1945 — Amy Hungerford (Yale)Read Foster quickly and playfully to start noticing patterns. Watch a few Hungerford lectures to see close reading done live; no need to read every novel she covers.
  2. Short stories firstMainSelected Stories — Anton ChekhovOne story per evening: quick wins that train attention. After each, write two sentences on what changed and how Chekhov showed it without saying it.
  3. Homeric epicMainIliad & Odyssey — HomerAlsoThe Iliad of Homer & The Odyssey of Homer — Elizabeth Vandiver (The Great Courses)Read Emily Wilson's translations, a book or two at a time, and watch Vandiver's matching lecture after each section. Start with the Odyssey if the Iliad's battles stall you.
  4. Greek tragedyMainThe Theban Plays — SophoclesRead Oedipus the King, then Antigone, ideally aloud in part. Each play fits a few evenings; notice how fate and choice collide.
  5. Dante's Divine ComedyMainThe Divine Comedy — DanteAlsoDante in Translation — Giuseppe Mazzotta (Yale)Read a few cantos with your edition's notes, then watch Mazzotta's lecture on them. Finishing Inferno is a fine milestone if Purgatorio and Paradiso must wait.
  6. Shakespeare on stageMainMajor tragedies & histories — ShakespeareAlsoShakespeare After All — Marjorie GarberRead Hamlet, King Lear, Macbeth and Henry IV in an annotated edition, then watch a good production. Read Garber's essay on each play after finishing it.
  7. Reading poetryMainHow to Read a Poem and Fall in Love with Poetry — Edward HirschAlsoModern Poetry — Langdon Hammer (Yale)PracticeThe Norton Anthology of Poetry — Margaret Ferguson et al. (eds.)Read Hirsch first to learn slow, pleasurable reading. Then read a few Norton poems daily, aloud; take Hammer's lectures to watch poems opened line by line.
  8. The first modern novelMainDon Quixote — CervantesAlsoCervantes' Don Quixote — Roberto González Echevarría (Yale)Read the novel part by part alongside the matching Echevarría lectures. It is long; a chapter or two per session keeps momentum.
  9. English realismMainMiddlemarch — George EliotAlsoHow Fiction Works — James WoodRead Wood's short book first to learn how narration and free indirect style work, then read Middlemarch slowly, watching Eliot move in and out of her characters' minds.
  10. Tolstoy and the RussiansMainAnna Karenina — TolstoyStart the Russians here, in a modern translation. Track the two plot lines, Anna's and Levin's, and ask why Tolstoy sets them side by side.
  11. Dostoevsky, firstMainCrime and Punishment — DostoevskyThe accessible Dostoevsky: a psychological thriller about an idea. Read it before attempting his larger novel.
  12. Dostoevsky's summitMainThe Brothers Karamazov — DostoevskyFaith, doubt and freedom at full depth. Read slowly; 'The Grand Inquisitor' chapter deserves a session of its own.
  13. Modernism with WoolfMainMrs Dalloway — Virginia WoolfOne London day inside several minds: the readable way into modernism. Read in long-ish stretches so the shifts between consciousnesses stay clear.
  14. Beyond EuropeMainThe Arabian Nights — Husain Haddawy (trans.)Read Shahrazad's frame tale, then a few nested stories at a time. From here, branch out to Asian, Middle Eastern and Latin American literature.
  15. Literary theory (optional)MainLiterary Theory: A Very Short Introduction — CullerAlsoIntroduction to Theory of Literature — Paul Fry (Yale)An optional capstone: read Culler's short book for the main critical questions, then take Fry's lectures if you want the schools of criticism in depth.
Then, by interest
  • Modern Drama — start with A Doll's House & Hedda Gabler — Henrik Ibsen
  • 20th-Century Fiction — start with The Great Gatsby — F. Scott Fitzgerald
  • 21st-Century Fiction — start with Wolf Hall — Hilary Mantel
  • Modern World Literature — start with One Hundred Years of Solitude — Gabriel García Márquez

Textbook path 5 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. How to Read Literature Like a Professor — FosterA gentle, playful first primer on symbols, patterns and recurring motifs; read it quickly to start noticing more, knowing later books on this path go deeper.
  2. How Fiction Works — James WoodThe deeper step after Foster: how narration, detail, character and free indirect style actually work. Short chapters — read one, then reread a novel passage with it.
  3. Rhyme's Reason — John HollanderYour guide to poetry's sound: English meter and verse forms, each explained in an example of itself. Read a few forms at a time, reading the examples aloud.
  4. Lectures on Literature — NabokovA great novelist's close readings of classic European novels, from Austen to Joyce. Read each lecture right after the novel it discusses, as Wood taught you to read.
  5. Literary Theory: A Very Short Introduction — CullerFinally, the main critical frameworks — what theory asks about meaning, language and identity — in one short, clear book. An optional capstone; pairs with Fry's lectures if wanted.
