Where value diverges

Translation changes the experience. For Homer, Emily Wilson is brisk and plain, Fagles grander; for the Russians, Pevear & Volokhonsky stay closest to the original's roughness, while the Maudes and Katz read more smoothly. One great novel finished beats three abandoned, so pace the long ones. Criticism (Wood, Fry, Nabokov) pays off after you have read some primaries, not instead of them.

Systems & Complexity

0 / 4 Essentials · 0 / 22

The synthesis layer that connects every domain above: feedback, nonlinearity, networks, emergence and information. Systems Thinking needs no prerequisites; Dynamics & Chaos and Networks want differential equations, linear algebra and probability.

Optimal path 8 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Thinking in systemsFirstNicky Case — explorables — Nicky CaseMainThinking in Systems — MeadowsRead Meadows whole, then play the matching Nicky Case explorables on feedback loops and emergence. Sketch a stock-and-flow diagram of something in your work.
  2. Guided tour of complexityMainIntroduction to Complexity — Melanie Mitchell (Santa Fe Institute)AlsoComplexity: A Guided Tour — MitchellTake Mitchell's self-paced course unit by unit, doing its exercises; read the matching chapters of her book for depth and context.
  3. Chaos on-rampMainIntroduction to Dynamical Systems and Chaos — David Feldman (Santa Fe Institute)Work through Feldman's gentle units on iterated maps, bifurcations, attractors and fractals. Do the quizzes; it prepares you for Strogatz, later on this path.
  4. Nonlinear dynamicsMainNonlinear Dynamics and Chaos — StrogatzAlsoNonlinear Dynamics and Chaos Lectures — Steven Strogatz (Cornell)Watch the lecture, then read the matching chapter and work a few exercises per section. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path; skip proofs on a first pass.
  5. Computation and natureMainThe Computational Beauty of Nature — Gary William FlakeRevisit Strogatz's chaos hands-on, plus fractals, cellular automata, genetic algorithms and neural nets. Write or run each program rather than only reading.
  6. Agent-based modellingMainAn Introduction to Agent-Based Modeling — Wilensky & RandPracticeNetLogo — Uri Wilensky (Northwestern)Build each model in NetLogo as you read: flocking, segregation, epidemics, markets. Then tweak one parameter and predict the outcome before you run it.
  7. Network scienceMainNetwork Science — BarabásiFree online: read the core chapters on random, scale-free and small-world networks, robustness and spreading, playing with the interactive figures.
  8. Networks, crowds and marketsMainNetworks, Crowds, and Markets — Easley & KleinbergRead selectively after Barabási for the social-science view: cascades, link analysis, search and auctions. Pick the chapters closest to your work.
Course path 6 steps
  1. CourseNicky Case — explorables — Nicky CasePlay the explorables on feedback loops, trust and emergence. Then sketch a stock-and-flow diagram of one system at work: a backlog, hiring, incidents.
  2. CourseIntroduction to Complexity — Melanie Mitchell (Santa Fe Institute)BookComplexity: A Guided Tour — MitchellTake Mitchell's self-paced course unit by unit, doing its exercises; read the matching chapters of her book for depth and context.
  3. CourseIntroduction to Dynamical Systems and Chaos — David Feldman (Santa Fe Institute)BookChaos: Making a New Science — James GleickWork Feldman's units on iterated maps, bifurcations, attractors and fractals, with the quizzes. Gleick's history of Lorenz, Feigenbaum and Mandelbrot is the bedtime companion.
  4. CourseNonlinear Dynamics and Chaos Lectures — Steven Strogatz (Cornell)One lecture per session: fixed points, bifurcations, limit cycles, chaos. Assumes calculus from the Mathematics path; redo each worked example yourself before moving on.
  5. CourseNetLogo — Uri Wilensky (Northwestern)BookMicromotives and Macrobehavior — Thomas SchellingRead Schelling on how individual choices add up to unintended patterns, then run and tweak NetLogo library models: segregation, flocking, epidemics. Predict before each run.
  6. BookLinked — Albert-László BarabásiHow scale-free and small-world networks were discovered, and why hubs matter for robustness and spreading. Revisit Mitchell's network units afterwards.
Textbook path 6 books

The same route as one textbook per stage, in order — for when you want to go deep from the page.

  1. Thinking in Systems — MeadowsStart here: stocks, flows, feedback loops, delays and leverage points in a short, clear primer. Read it whole; sketch a stock-and-flow diagram of something in your work.
  2. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos — StrogatzThe core maths of change: fixed points, bifurcations, limit cycles, chaos and fractals, applied and visual. Work some exercises per section; assumes calculus from the Mathematics path.
  3. The Computational Beauty of Nature — Gary William FlakeComputation as a lens: fractals, chaos, cellular automata, genetic algorithms and neural nets explored by writing programs. Revisits Strogatz's chaos hands-on; run the programs.
  4. An Introduction to Agent-Based Modeling — Wilensky & RandBuild emergence yourself in NetLogo: flocking, segregation, epidemics and markets. Build each model as you read rather than just running the examples.
  5. Network Science — BarabásiFree online: random, scale-free and small-world networks, robustness, communities and spreading. Read the core chapters with the interactive figures.
  6. Networks, Crowds, and Markets — Easley & KleinbergFree online: networks meet game theory and markets — cascades, link analysis, search and auctions. Read selectively after Barabási for the social-science view.

Where value diverges

Meadows and Mitchell give the vocabulary; Strogatz is where it becomes mathematics you can use — do his book with the Cornell lectures. Barabási's Network Science is the readable text, Newman the rigorous reference. Popular books here (Gleick, West, Schelling) are motivation, not method. Treat claims of universal laws with care: scaling laws and self-organized criticality are live research with real disputes, not settled fact.

The Curiosity Shelf

0 / 10 Essentials · 0 / 149

The motivation and wonder layer: popular science, channels, narratives and fiction of ideas, organised by field to sit beside your STEM study. Read one at a time, about 20 minutes before bed; these build momentum and intuition, not rigour. See these paired with concepts in the STEM Atlas ↗

Optimal path 12 stages

The best way through: for each stage, the most teachable resource (course or book) as Main, with a quick intuition-builder to start and a place to practise.

  1. Mathematics made visibleMain3Blue1Brown — Grant SandersonAlsoJourney Through Genius — DunhamWatch one 3Blue1Brown series at a time and pause to predict the next step. Read Dunham's great theorems, one per evening, to see the proofs and the people behind them.
  2. How a physicist thinksFirstVeritasium — Derek MullerMainSix Easy Pieces — FeynmanWatch a Veritasium video to get a misconception exposed, then read a Feynman chapter for the real picture. One chapter per session is plenty.
  3. Data and uncertaintyMainThe Art of Statistics — David SpiegelhalterPracticeSeeing Theory — Brown UniversityRead Spiegelhalter for how to learn from data without fooling yourself; play with the matching Seeing Theory visualisations to make sampling and uncertainty tangible.
  4. The story of scienceFirstCrash Course History of Science — Hank GreenMainA Short History of Nearly Everything — Bill BrysonRead Bryson as an evening companion; watch Crash Course History of Science episodes to place each discovery in its era.
  5. Scale of the cosmosFirstCrash Course Astronomy — Phil PlaitMainCosmos — SaganPracticeKerbal Space Program — SquadWatch Crash Course Astronomy in order for the facts, read Cosmos for the sweep and wonder. Fly orbits in Kerbal if you want orbital mechanics in your hands.
  6. The elementsFirstNileRed — Nigel BraunMainThe Disappearing Spoon — Sam KeanRead Kean's periodic-table stories; watch NileRed to see real chemistry done step by step in a lab.
  7. Evolution in your bodyFirstJourney to the Microcosmos — Hank Green & James WeissMainYour Inner Fish — Neil ShubinRead Shubin to trace your anatomy back to fish. Watch Microcosmos episodes to see living cells and microbes, the small end of the same story.
  8. Evolution's great inventionsMainLife Ascending — Nick LaneTen inventions of evolution at current-science depth; denser than Shubin. Read one chapter per session and summarise it in a few sentences.
  9. Codes and secretsFirstComputerphile — Sean RileyMainThe Code Book — Simon SinghRead Singh's history of codes and try its puzzles. Watch Computerphile videos on encryption to connect the history to how it works today.
  10. How machines learnFirstWelch Labs — Stephen WelchMainWhy Machines Learn — Anil AnanthaswamyWatch Welch Labs' neural-network videos to see the mathematics move, then read Ananthaswamy's chapters on perceptrons, gradient descent and networks.
  11. Self-reference and mindsMainGödel, Escher, Bach — HofstadterRead slowly over months, a dialogue and chapter at a time. Skim the denser formal-system sections on a first pass if they stall you.
  12. Fiction of ideasMainStories of Your Life and Others — Ted ChiangOne story per evening. Each is built on a real idea from linguistics, physics or mathematics; afterwards, name the idea and how the story used it.

Channels and short books work best alongside active study; long narratives (Rhodes, Gödel, Escher, Bach, Behave) reward a dedicated stretch. Older classics are flagged where the science has moved on. The fiction teaches ideas and wonder, not facts: treat history-based novels such as Labatut's as invention and check details in the non-fiction.
